Attempt 1
Question 1Correct

Deploying a code update to a production Amazon Elastic Beanstalk environment must prioritize the ability to roll back quickly above every other consideration, including cost and deployment speed. Truenorth Council, a consumer electronics manufacturer whose order-processing platform cannot tolerate extended downtime, needs to select the deployment policy that satisfies this requirement for its upcoming release.

Which deployment policy should Truenorth Council's development team choose?

Rolling with additional batch

Explanation

Incorrect. Rolling with additional batch launches one extra batch of instances before the rolling update starts. This extra batch helps the environment keep full capacity during deployment. The policy still modifies the original fleet in place, the same way standard rolling deployments do. If the update fails, recovery still requires manually redeploying the previous version instead of an instant rollback. Keyword tip: this policy protects capacity during deployment, but it still lacks the instant-rollback safety of a separate, untouched environment.
Your answer is correct
Immutable

Explanation

Correct. The Immutable deployment policy launches an entirely new, separate set of instances in a temporary Auto Scaling group. The new instances receive the updated application version and must pass health checks before any traffic shifts to them. The original instances keep running unmodified during this entire process. If the new version fails its health checks, rollback is nearly instant, because the original fleet never stopped serving traffic and no redeployment is needed. Keyword tip: 'Immutable' costs more and takes longer to deploy, but it delivers zero downtime and the fastest, safest rollback, which makes it the right choice when rollback speed is the top priority for a production-critical workload.
All at once

Explanation

Incorrect. All at once deploys the new application version to every instance at the same time. This approach causes downtime during the update. If the deployment fails, there is no fallback instance set available, so recovery requires manually redeploying the previous version. Keyword tip: 'All at once' is the fastest and cheapest policy, but it is also the riskiest, because it offers zero rollback safety and causes an outage.
Rolling

Explanation

Incorrect. Rolling deployments update instances in batches inside the existing Auto Scaling group. During the update, the environment runs a mix of old and new application versions at the same time. If the new version fails, there is no separate set of untouched original instances to fall back to. Recovery requires a manual redeployment of the previous version. Keyword tip: 'Rolling' updates instances in place and does not provide a fast, built-in rollback path.

AWS Elastic Beanstalk deployment policies each optimize for a different combination of cost, deployment speed, downtime, and rollback safety, and choosing correctly means identifying which of these constraints the scenario values most. All at once is fastest and cheapest but causes downtime and has no rollback safety net. Rolling and Rolling with additional batch reduce downtime by updating instances in smaller groups, but both modify the original fleet in place, so recovering from a bad deployment still requires a manual redeployment of the previous version. Immutable is the slowest and most expensive policy, because it stands up an entirely separate, parallel set of instances, but this separation is exactly what makes rollback nearly instant: the original fleet never stops running until the new version proves healthy.

Use case: A consumer electronics manufacturer like Truenorth Council might run its production order-processing environment on Elastic Beanstalk with the Immutable policy specifically because any failed deployment during a peak sales period could otherwise disrupt order intake for customers and retail partners. By keeping the original fleet fully intact until the new version passes health checks, the team can revert to the previous, known-good version almost instantly if problems appear, protecting order continuity.

References:

https://docs.aws.amazon.com/elasticbeanstalk/latest/dg/using-features.deploy-existing-version.html
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/elasticbeanstalk/latest/dg/using-features.rolling-version-deploy.html

Question 2Correct

The compound registry team at Stonebridge Group, a pharmaceutical research organization, currently relies on an Amazon ElastiCache caching layer placed in front of its backend compound database to speed up read access for scientists querying experimental compound records. A new regulatory requirement now mandates that any update to compound safety data must be immediately and consistently reflected in both the cache and the backend database, while still maintaining low-latency read performance for every record stored in the database.

Which cache writing policy will satisfy these requirements?

Invalidate the cache for each database write.

Explanation

Incorrect. Invalidating the cache entry after each database write removes the item from the cache. The next read for that item becomes a cache miss and requires a trip to the backend database to reload the data into the cache. This approach does not guarantee low latency for all items, because recently updated items suffer a read penalty until the cache is repopulated. Keyword tip: cache invalidation on write removes stale data but sacrifices read latency, so it does not match a requirement for low latency on all items.
Add a short duration TTL value to each write.

Explanation

Incorrect. A short time-to-live (TTL) value controls when a cached item expires. Adding a TTL does not update the cache at the moment the backend database is written. Because of this delay, the cache can hold stale data until the TTL expires. Keyword tip: TTL-based expiration reduces staleness over time, but it does not provide immediate, strong consistency.
Your answer is correct
Use a write-through caching strategy.

Explanation

Correct. A write-through caching strategy writes data to the cache and the backend database at the same time. This keeps the cache always up to date and consistent with the database. Because every record is written to the cache during a write operation, every record stays available in the cache and can be read with low latency. Keyword tip: look for the phrase "write-through" when a scenario needs strong consistency and low-latency reads for all items.
Use a lazy-loading caching strategy.

Explanation

Incorrect. A lazy-loading (cache-aside) strategy only loads data into the cache when an application requests the data and the data is not already in the cache. Updates to the backend database are not automatically pushed to the cache under this strategy. Because of this, the cache can serve stale data until the entry expires or is reloaded after a cache miss. Keyword tip: lazy loading only populates the cache on read misses, which creates a consistency gap right after a write.

This question tests knowledge of Amazon ElastiCache caching strategies and the trade-off between consistency and latency. A write-through strategy writes data to the cache and the database at the same time. This strategy keeps the cache strongly consistent with the database and guarantees that every item is available in the cache for low-latency reads, at the cost of extra latency during each write operation. A lazy-loading (cache-aside) strategy and a short TTL value both reduce write overhead, but both allow temporary staleness, because the cache is only updated on a read miss or after the TTL expires. Cache invalidation on write removes stale data immediately, but it forces a cache miss on the next read, which reintroduces a latency penalty. When a scenario requires both strong consistency and low latency for every item, write-through is the correct strategy despite its added write cost.

A similar situation: Stonebridge Group's compound registry system must guarantee that when a lab scientist updates a compound's safety profile, every subsequent read of that compound - whether it is a newly registered compound or one that has existed in the system for years - returns the updated data instantly and without extra database round trips. A write-through cache achieves this by updating the cache and the database together on every write, so scientists never see outdated safety information while still getting fast read responses from the cache.

References:

https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonElastiCache/latest/mem-ug/Strategies.html

Question 3Correct

Quarrystone Logistics, the internal logistics and supply-chain department of a public university, currently runs an Amazon ECS cluster on Amazon EC2 container instances of several different instance types to support its course-material distribution and campus shipping systems. The department is now migrating a large number of additional Docker containers onto this existing cluster, and it must choose a task placement strategy that minimizes the number of container instances used based on available memory.

Which task placement strategy meets this requirement?

random

Explanation

Incorrect. The random strategy places tasks on container instances chosen at random. Random placement does not consider CPU or memory usage on any instance. Random placement does not try to pack tasks onto fewer instances. Keyword tip: treat "random" as offering no optimization logic, so it is rarely correct when a question states an efficiency or cost goal.
spread

Explanation

Incorrect. The spread strategy places tasks evenly across a specified value, such as instance ID or Availability Zone. This spreads the workload across many hosts to improve high availability. Spread does not consolidate tasks onto fewer instances. Because the requirement is to minimize the number of instances used, spread does not meet the requirement. Keyword tip: connect the word "spread" with even distribution and high availability, not with consolidation.
distinctInstance

Explanation

Incorrect. distinctInstance is a task placement constraint, not a task placement strategy. A constraint using distinctInstance forces each task in a group to run on a separate container instance. This isolates workloads, but it increases the number of instances used instead of reducing it. Keyword tip: remember that constraints (distinctInstance, memberOf) limit where a task can run, while strategies (binpack, random, spread) decide how ECS chooses among the eligible instances.
Your answer is correct
binpack

Explanation

Correct. The binpack strategy places each task on the container instance that has the least available CPU or memory remaining, after ECS accounts for the resources the task needs. This packs tasks tightly onto as few instances as possible. Because Quarrystone Logistics needs to minimize the number of container instances based on available memory, binpack is the correct strategy. Keyword tip: when a question asks to minimize the number of instances or maximize resource utilization on an ECS cluster using the EC2 launch type, binpack is the strategy being tested.

Amazon ECS task placement strategies and constraints apply only to tasks that use the EC2 launch type. Fargate tasks are placed automatically across Availability Zones and do not support custom placement strategies. Binpack places each new task on the instance with the least available CPU or memory, so it packs tasks tightly and minimizes the number of instances in use. Spread distributes tasks evenly across a chosen value to increase availability, random selects instances without any optimization logic, and distinctInstance is a constraint that forces task separation for isolation rather than a strategy for consolidation. The correct choice always depends on matching the stated goal, such as cost reduction, high availability, or isolation, to the matching strategy or constraint.

Practical example: A university IT department running many small internal services, such as library catalog lookups or campus shuttle tracking APIs, on a mixed-instance-type ECS cluster can use the binpack strategy to consolidate those services onto the fewest EC2 container instances possible. This reduces the number of running instances and lowers infrastructure cost, since ECS fills each instance's remaining memory before starting a new one.

References:

https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonECS/latest/developerguide/task-placement-strategies.html

Question 4Correct

A gradual, low-risk rollout of a new API version to a limited slice of production traffic requires a mechanism that avoids custom traffic-splitting logic. Prairiewind Associates, a healthcare diagnostics provider whose mobile application lets patients view lab results through Amazon API Gateway, needs to introduce an updated API version to a small subset of users before a full release.

What is the MOST straightforward method for the company to introduce the new API version to a subset of users through API Gateway?

Deploy the new API in a separate VPC and use Amazon CloudFront to distribute the API traffic between the old and new versions

Explanation

Incorrect. Deploying the new API in a separate VPC and using Amazon CloudFront to distribute traffic adds significant architectural complexity. This approach requires a separate network and additional distribution configuration. It does not provide the simple, percentage-based traffic control that API Gateway's canary deployment feature already offers out of the box. Keyword tip: an answer that requires a 'separate VPC' or an extra infrastructure layer is rarely the 'MOST straightforward' choice when a native feature already exists.
Your answer is correct
Utilize the canary release deployment feature in API Gateway. Configure the canarySettings to redirect a portion of the API traffic

Explanation

Correct. API Gateway's canary release deployment feature lets a developer deploy a new API version to a canary stage. The developer sets the canarySettings percentTraffic parameter to send a chosen percentage of requests to that canary stage. This feature gives a controlled, gradual rollout, and the developer can promote the canary to full production or roll it back easily. Keyword tip: the terms 'canarySettings' and 'percentTraffic' inside API Gateway point directly to the built-in canary release mechanism.
Develop a custom Lambda function to control the API traffic distribution between the two API versions

Explanation

Incorrect. Building a custom Lambda function to split and route traffic between API versions adds unnecessary complexity. This approach requires the developer to write and maintain custom routing logic. It also duplicates a capability that API Gateway already provides natively through canary releases. Keyword tip: when a question describes writing custom code to control traffic splitting, check first whether a native service feature already solves the same problem more simply.
Use an Amazon Route 53 failover routing policy to divert a certain percentage of traffic to the updated API version

Explanation

Incorrect. Amazon Route 53 failover routing sends traffic to a backup resource only when a health check detects that the primary resource is unavailable. Route 53 failover does not split traffic by percentage between two active versions of an API. This routing policy is built for disaster recovery, not for a controlled rollout. Keyword tip: the phrase 'failover routing policy' signals health-check-based disaster recovery, not gradual rollout or percentage-based traffic splitting.

This question tests knowledge of API Gateway's canary release deployment feature. This feature is the native, purpose-built mechanism for sending a chosen percentage of traffic to a new API version before a full rollout. A developer should use canary releases whenever the goal is a controlled, percentage-based rollout with an easy path to promote or roll back the change. Route 53 failover routing is built for disaster recovery, and custom Lambda functions or separate VPC and CloudFront architectures add complexity that is not needed when API Gateway already provides this capability natively.

Applied example: Prairiewind Associates, a healthcare diagnostics provider, needs to test a new version of the API behind its patient results mobile application before sending it to every patient. The development team configures a canary stage in API Gateway and sets percentTraffic to a small value, such as 5 percent. This lets the team monitor the new API version with real traffic from a small group of patients, and the team can roll back instantly if an error rate rises, before promoting the change to all users.

References:

https://docs.aws.amazon.com/apigateway/latest/developerguide/canary-release.html

Question 5Correct

Upgrading a Node.js platform version while deploying new application code must happen without any downtime for a high-traffic clinical trial data portal. Greystone Group, a pharmaceutical research organization headquartered in Boston, runs this website on Amazon EC2 instances managed by AWS Elastic Beanstalk, and its engineering team needs to introduce a new feature that requires the newer Node.js runtime.

Which strategy should the team adopt to fulfill these requirements?

Create a duplicate EC2 instance manually with the new version of Node.js and the updated code. Test the new instance and replace one of the instances behind the load balancer once the testing is successful.

Explanation

Incorrect. This option replaces EC2 instances manually behind the load balancer instead of using Elastic Beanstalk's deployment features. Manual instance replacement is error-prone and difficult to test or roll back consistently at scale. Elastic Beanstalk-managed environment swaps are more reliable because they are automated and repeatable. Keyword tip: manual, ad hoc instance replacement outside of the deployment platform's tooling is usually the least reliable choice in these scenarios.
Your answer is correct
Implement Blue/Green (CNAME swap) deployment using Elastic Beanstalk. Prepare a separate environment with the new version of Node.js and the new code, and once testing is complete, swap the CNAMEs of the two environments.

Explanation

Correct. Blue/Green deployment in Elastic Beanstalk creates a separate green environment that runs the new Node.js platform version and the new application code. The team tests the green environment fully before it receives any production traffic, while the original blue environment keeps serving users during testing. After testing succeeds, the team swaps the environment CNAMEs, and this swap causes no downtime. Keyword tip: the terms "Blue/Green" and "CNAME swap" together identify the standard Elastic Beanstalk pattern for zero-downtime platform and code changes.
Upgrade the platform version of the current Elastic Beanstalk environment, then deploy the new application code. Monitor the application and quickly roll back changes if any issues occur.

Explanation

Incorrect. This option upgrades the platform version on the currently running environment before deploying the new code. A platform version upgrade generally requires replacing or restarting the environment's instances, which can cause downtime. If a problem occurs after the upgrade, rolling back causes another service interruption. Keyword tip: relying on monitoring and rollback as the safety net signals that a strategy is not zero-downtime by design.
Use AWS CodeDeploy to deploy the new application code first, then manually update Node.js on the Elastic Beanstalk environment.

Explanation

Incorrect. This option deploys the new application code first and updates the Node.js platform manually afterward. Updating the platform version usually requires restarting the underlying EC2 instances. Restarting the instances interrupts traffic on the current environment. This approach does not guarantee zero downtime. Keyword tip: any strategy that changes the platform of the currently live environment in place is a warning sign for downtime risk.

This question tests knowledge of Elastic Beanstalk deployment strategies for zero-downtime platform and application upgrades. Blue/Green deployment with a CNAME swap is the preferred approach when the platform version and the application code both need to change at the same time. This approach lets the team fully test the new environment before any production traffic reaches it, and the CNAME swap itself causes no interruption to end users. In-place platform upgrades, manual instance replacement, and rollback-based strategies all carry downtime risk because they modify or restart the live environment's instances directly.

Applied example: Greystone Group, a pharmaceutical research organization, must roll out a new feature on its clinical trial data portal that requires a newer Node.js runtime. The engineering team creates a separate Elastic Beanstalk environment with the new Node.js version and the new code, validates it against test data, and swaps the environment CNAME once validation passes. Researchers and partner labs accessing the portal experience no interruption during the entire upgrade process.

References:

https://docs.aws.amazon.com/elasticbeanstalk/latest/dg/using-features.CNAMESwap.html

Question 6Incorrect

A nightly reporting job must scan a large Amazon DynamoDB table to generate a usage summary, and the scan needs to finish faster without disrupting live traffic. Ivywood Networks, a video conferencing SaaS company that runs this job during off-peak hours, currently sees production traffic consume around 50% of the table's provisioned read capacity even during the scan window.

Which two actions should a developer take to minimize the time required to produce the report without affecting production workloads? (Select TWO.)

Correct selection
Use the Limit parameter

Explanation

Correct. The Limit parameter sets the maximum number of items that a single Scan request returns. This setting stops one worker in a parallel scan from consuming all of the table's available read capacity. The Limit parameter protects the other workers and the production traffic from being starved of throughput. Keyword tip: look for phrases like "throttling protection" or "rate-limiting during a scan" as signals to use the Limit parameter together with parallel scan segments.
Your selection is incorrect
Use a Sequential Scan API operation

Explanation

Incorrect. A sequential scan processes the table one segment at a time. A sequential scan is limited by the throughput available to that single segment, so the scan takes longer to finish. This behavior directly conflicts with the goal of minimizing scan time. Keyword tip: "Sequential Scan" describes the default, slower behavior and is rarely the correct choice when the goal is to minimize scan duration.
Your selection is incorrect
Increase read capacity units during the scan operation

Explanation

Incorrect. Increasing read capacity units would make the scan run faster, but it raises cost. Increasing read capacity units does not address the requirement to use the existing provisioned throughput efficiently without affecting production traffic. Keyword tip: treat any option that adds more provisioned capacity to fix a performance problem as a cost-inefficient shortcut, not the best-practice answer.
Correct selection
Use a Parallel Scan API operation

Explanation

Correct. The Parallel Scan API operation divides the table or index into multiple logical segments. Multiple workers scan different segments at the same time, which overcomes the throughput limit of scanning one segment sequentially. This approach significantly reduces the total time needed to complete the scan. Keyword tip: phrases like "divide into segments" and "multiple workers scanning concurrently" point to Parallel Scan.
Use pagination to divide results into pages sized at DynamoDB's default per-request data limit

Explanation

Incorrect. Pagination is simply how DynamoDB returns Scan results by default, dividing output into fixed-size response pages. Pagination does not distribute the scan workload across partitions and does not limit throughput consumption per worker, so it does not help minimize scan time or protect production throughput. Keyword tip: pagination controls how results are retrieved, not how work is parallelized or throttled.

This question tests the ability to optimize a DynamoDB Scan operation so that it finishes faster while protecting the provisioned throughput that production traffic needs. A sequential scan reads one segment at a time and is limited by the throughput of that single segment, so it is only appropriate for small tables or when speed is not a priority. A parallel scan divides the table into multiple segments and lets multiple workers scan those segments at the same time, which is the correct approach when the goal is to finish a scan on a large table quickly. The Limit parameter caps how many items each worker request returns, which prevents any single worker from consuming all of the throughput and starving the other workers or the production workload. The correct combination is parallel scan for speed and the Limit parameter for throughput control, while increasing capacity or relying on default pagination does not solve the actual constraint in this scenario.

Consider this scenario: Ivywood Networks runs a nightly usage report against a DynamoDB table that stores video conferencing session metadata for thousands of active meetings. Running a single sequential scan during business hours would compete with live meeting traffic for the same read capacity, causing latency for users joining or managing calls. By switching to a parallel scan with a bounded Limit parameter per worker, the engineering team finishes the report in a fraction of the time while keeping enough throughput available for production API calls.

References:

https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/developer/rate-limited-scans-in-amazon-dynamodb/
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/Scan.html#Scan.ParallelScan

Question 7Incorrect

Eastwick Systems needs to roll out a new feature to a small group of beta testers without affecting the experience of its existing users, as part of a serverless application it operates for a public university with a large, active student body. The new feature involves an AWS Lambda function that is invoked by an Amazon API Gateway API, and the API currently uses a specific Lambda alias to invoke the function.

What would be the most efficient approach to meet these requirements?

Correct answer
Create a new version of the Lambda function. Build a new stage on API Gateway integrated with this new Lambda version. Utilize this new API Gateway stage for beta testing.

Explanation

Correct. Publishing a new Lambda version creates an immutable snapshot of the function code. Creating a new API Gateway stage that points to this new Lambda version gives beta testers a separate endpoint to call. Existing users keep using the original stage and alias, so their experience does not change. Keyword tip: a dedicated API Gateway stage mapped to a new Lambda version is the standard pattern for isolated beta testing.
Use the AWS CLI to manually switch between the old and new versions of the Lambda function during testing periods.

Explanation

Incorrect. Manually switching between Lambda versions with the AWS CLI requires a person to perform the switch every time. This approach is slow and prone to human error. It also does not separate beta testers from existing users, because everyone still calls the same Lambda alias. Keyword tip: manual CLI switching for production traffic control is a sign of an inefficient, unmanaged approach.
Your answer is incorrect
Use AWS CodeDeploy to deploy the updated Lambda function. Split traffic between the new and old versions of the function for testing purposes.

Explanation

Incorrect. AWS CodeDeploy can shift a percentage of traffic from one Lambda version to another. This capability is useful for canary or linear deployments that reduce risk during a production rollout. AWS CodeDeploy does not let you target a specific, known group of beta users; it only shifts a random percentage of all traffic. Keyword tip: CodeDeploy traffic shifting supports gradual production rollout, not isolation of a defined beta group.
Implement Amazon S3 bucket versioning on the Lambda function code. For testing purposes, link the API Gateway to the new version of the code stored in the S3 bucket.

Explanation

Incorrect. Amazon S3 bucket versioning tracks different versions of objects stored in a bucket. API Gateway cannot invoke a Lambda function directly from a specific S3 object version. This option confuses S3 object versioning with Lambda function versioning, which are separate and unrelated features. Keyword tip: S3 versioning applies to stored objects, not to Lambda function versions or API Gateway routing.

This question tests knowledge of AWS Lambda versions and aliases combined with Amazon API Gateway stages as a way to isolate a small group of users for testing. A Lambda version is an immutable snapshot of function code. An API Gateway stage can point to a specific Lambda version or alias, so you can create a separate stage for beta testers while the production stage keeps serving existing users unchanged. AWS CodeDeploy shifts a percentage of traffic between Lambda versions during a deployment, which is useful for gradual, population-wide rollouts, but it cannot target a specific, known group of users. The correct choice depends on whether the requirement is precise audience isolation, which favors a dedicated stage, or gradual rollout to an unknown population, which favors CodeDeploy traffic shifting.

Real-world example: Eastwick Systems, a public university, could use this pattern to test a new course-registration feature with a small group of faculty advisors before releasing it to the entire student body. The advisors would use a separate API Gateway stage that points to the new Lambda version, while students continue using the stable production stage. This setup keeps the beta test isolated and prevents any disruption to the live registration system during peak enrollment periods.

References:

https://docs.aws.amazon.com/apigateway/latest/developerguide/set-up-stages.html

Question 8Incorrect

Eastwick Agency, a music streaming platform headquartered in Austin, Texas, is building a new listener-facing application that must support Security Assertion Markup Language (SAML) authentication as well as sign-in through social identity providers such as Google or Facebook. The application also needs authorization to directly access listener data stored in Amazon S3 buckets and Amazon DynamoDB tables.

Which AWS service or feature will meet these requirements with the LEAST amount of additional coding?

Amazon API Gateway REST API

Explanation

Incorrect. Amazon API Gateway REST API is used to expose and manage APIs. Amazon API Gateway does not authenticate users against SAML or social identity providers, and it does not issue AWS credentials on its own. Building a custom REST API layer to bridge authentication and AWS access would require significantly more coding than a managed federation service. Keyword tip: Amazon API Gateway handles API routing, throttling, and management, not identity federation or credential vending.
AWS AppSync GraphQL API

Explanation

Incorrect. AWS AppSync provides a managed GraphQL API layer for querying and updating data. AWS AppSync does not solve an authentication-and-authorization problem by itself. Adding AWS AppSync here would introduce unnecessary development work instead of reducing it. Keyword tip: AWS AppSync is for building GraphQL APIs with resolvers and real-time data sync, not for issuing AWS credentials to authenticated users.
Your answer is incorrect
Amazon Cognito user pools

Explanation

Incorrect. Amazon Cognito user pools handle user authentication. A user pool can accept sign-in through SAML and through social identity providers. A user pool does not give an application temporary AWS credentials. To reach Amazon S3 or DynamoDB, Eastwick Agency would still need to pair the user pool with an identity pool. This pairing adds extra coding, so this option does not meet the LEAST-coding requirement. Keyword tip: user pools handle authentication and sign-up/sign-in; identity pools handle authorization and AWS credentials.
Correct answer
Amazon Cognito identity pools

Explanation

Correct. Amazon Cognito identity pools, also called federated identities, accept identities from SAML providers, social identity providers, OpenID Connect providers, Amazon Cognito user pools, or developer-authenticated identities. An identity pool exchanges these identities for temporary, limited-privilege AWS credentials through AWS STS. Eastwick Agency's application can use these credentials to access Amazon S3 and DynamoDB directly, without writing custom authorization logic. Keyword tip: when a scenario needs AWS resource access after SAML, social, or federated sign-in, Amazon Cognito identity pools is the correct choice.

This question tests the difference between Amazon Cognito user pools and Amazon Cognito identity pools. Amazon Cognito user pools act as a user directory and handle authentication, including sign-in through SAML and through social identity providers. Amazon Cognito identity pools handle authorization: an identity pool takes an already-authenticated identity and exchanges it for temporary, limited-privilege AWS credentials through AWS STS. Use identity pools whenever an application needs direct, scoped access to AWS services such as Amazon S3 or DynamoDB after a user signs in through SAML, social, or other federated identity providers, because identity pools support many identity provider types natively and require minimal custom code.

A similar situation: Eastwick Agency wants listeners to sign in with their existing Google account or through their record label's SAML-based single sign-on, then have the mobile application read and write playlist data stored in DynamoDB and stream album art stored in S3. By placing an Amazon Cognito identity pool behind the sign-in flow, Eastwick Agency avoids building a custom authorization server and instead lets AWS STS issue temporary credentials scoped to exactly the S3 and DynamoDB resources each listener is allowed to use.

Question 9Incorrect

Truenorth Dynamics, a biotechnology research lab, operates a genomic sequencing pipeline on Amazon EC2 that produces a high volume of small metadata files, each about 1 KB in size, containing personally identifiable information about research subjects that must be converted to ciphertext. The lab stores these files on an in-house, proprietary network-attached storage appliance that has no native integration with AWS KMS.

What is the SAFEST way to encrypt the data using AWS KMS?

Correct answer
Encrypt the data directly with a customer managed customer master key

Explanation

Correct. A customer managed customer master key is created and fully controlled by the customer, including its key policy, IAM permissions, grants, rotation schedule, and deletion timeline. Each file is only 1 KB, which is within the 4 KB limit for direct encryption through the KMS Encrypt API, so no data encryption key is needed. Because the key material of a customer managed customer master key never leaves AWS KMS, this method gives the strongest security guarantee with the least operational complexity for small files. Keyword tip: when payload size is at or below 4 KB and the scenario requires full customer control over the key, encrypt the data directly with a customer managed customer master key.
Create a data encryption key from a customer master key and encrypt the data with the customer master key

Explanation

Incorrect. This option creates a data encryption key from a customer master key, but then encrypts the file with the customer master key instead of the data encryption key. Creating the data encryption key serves no purpose in this workflow, because the file is never encrypted with it. This wastes an extra API call to AWS KMS without adding any security benefit. Keyword tip: watch for options where a data encryption key is generated but the actual encryption step still uses the customer master key directly; this signals a broken envelope encryption workflow.
Your answer is incorrect
Create a data encryption key from a customer master key and encrypt the data with the data encryption key

Explanation

Incorrect. Creating a data encryption key from a customer master key and using the data encryption key to encrypt the data is the standard envelope encryption pattern. This pattern is designed for large files or high-volume encryption, because a customer master key can only encrypt up to 4 KB of data directly. Each file in this scenario is only 1 KB, so it fits within the direct encryption limit, and adding a separately managed data encryption key only increases operational risk without any benefit. Keyword tip: choose envelope encryption with a data encryption key only when data exceeds 4 KB or when the workload has high-volume or high-performance encryption needs.
Encrypt the data directly with an AWS managed customer master key

Explanation

Incorrect. An AWS managed customer master key is created and controlled by an AWS service, such as Amazon S3 or Amazon EBS, when that service needs to encrypt data on the customer's behalf. Truenorth Dynamics stores its files on a proprietary, non-AWS network-attached storage system, so no AWS service exists to request or manage an AWS managed customer master key for this data. Keyword tip: an AWS managed customer master key only appears when a supported AWS service creates it automatically; proprietary or unsupported storage systems cannot use one.

AWS KMS supports two main encryption approaches: direct encryption with a customer master key, and envelope encryption with a data encryption key. Direct encryption works only for payloads up to 4 KB per operation, but it keeps the key material inside AWS KMS at all times, making it the safest option for small files. Envelope encryption is required for larger data volumes, but it forces the customer to manage the data encryption key's lifecycle outside of AWS KMS, which adds operational risk. The choice between an AWS managed customer master key and a customer managed customer master key depends on who needs control: AWS managed keys only exist for specific AWS service integrations, while customer managed keys give the customer full control and work with any storage system, including non-AWS systems.

Real-world example: A biotechnology research lab like Truenorth Dynamics generates thousands of small metadata files during genomic sequencing runs, each containing personally identifiable information about research participants. Because these files are stored on an in-house network-attached storage appliance with no native AWS integration, the lab cannot rely on an AWS managed customer master key. Encrypting each file directly with a customer managed customer master key lets the lab's security team retain full control over key policies and rotation while meeting strict data privacy requirements for research subject data.

Question 10Correct

Sablecrest Trust must deploy a new version of its production application on AWS Elastic Beanstalk without causing any downtime for users, and any failed update must be reverted quickly and cleanly. The company operates a social media analytics platform that processes live engagement metrics for enterprise clients, so continuous availability is critical.

Which deployment method should be used?

Incremental

Explanation

Incorrect. Incremental is not a real Elastic Beanstalk deployment policy. The valid deployment policies are All at once, Rolling, Rolling with additional batch, Immutable, and Traffic splitting. Keyword tip: if an answer names a deployment policy that does not match one of these five official Elastic Beanstalk policies, treat it as a distractor.
Rolling

Explanation

Incorrect. A rolling deployment updates instances in batches. Each batch is taken out of service while it updates, so the environment loses capacity during the update. If the new version fails, Elastic Beanstalk needs a second rolling deployment to roll back, so the rollback is slow. Keyword tip: rolling deployments reduce capacity temporarily and roll back slowly, so they do not satisfy a strict zero-downtime, fast-rollback requirement.
All at once

Explanation

Incorrect. An all-at-once deployment updates every instance at the same time. The entire environment goes out of service during the update, so this policy causes downtime. Elastic Beanstalk does not provide an automatic rollback mechanism for this policy, so recovery from a failed update requires a new deployment. Keyword tip: all at once is the fastest deployment policy, but it causes full downtime and offers no built-in rollback.
Your answer is correct
Immutable

Explanation

Correct. An immutable deployment launches a completely new set of instances in a new Auto Scaling group. Elastic Beanstalk deploys the new application version to these new instances and checks their health before shifting traffic to them. The original environment keeps running and serving traffic until the new instances pass health checks, so there is zero downtime. If the new version fails validation, Elastic Beanstalk terminates the new instances and the new Auto Scaling group, so rollback is fast and low-risk. Keyword tip: choose immutable deployments when a scenario requires both zero downtime and a fast, safe rollback.

This question tests knowledge of AWS Elastic Beanstalk deployment policies and their trade-offs between downtime, deployment speed, and rollback complexity. Use All at once when downtime is acceptable and speed matters more than availability. Use Rolling or Rolling with additional batch when the environment can tolerate reduced capacity but does not require zero downtime. Use Immutable when the environment must have zero downtime and needs a fast, reliable rollback, because Immutable keeps the old environment running until the new instances pass health checks and simply terminates the new instances if they fail. Traffic splitting also supports zero downtime through canary-style testing, but it does not isolate the new version in a fully separate environment the way Immutable does.

Consider this scenario: Sablecrest Trust needs to update its live analytics dashboard application without interrupting service for clients who monitor social media engagement in real time. An Immutable deployment lets the company validate the new version on a separate set of instances before any client traffic reaches it, and lets the company revert instantly by terminating the new instances if a defect appears.

Question 11Incorrect

Larkspur Robotics needs to let users sign in to its new web application from any source, while automatically blocking any sign-in attempt that is flagged as high risk. The company, which supplies robotics kits and curriculum to K-12 school districts, uses Amazon Cognito to handle authentication for this application.

Which Amazon Cognito feature will meet these requirements?

Advanced security metrics

Explanation

Incorrect. Advanced security metrics send sign-in attempt data, risk levels, and failed challenge information to Amazon CloudWatch. This data supports monitoring and analysis. Advanced security metrics do not take any automated action to block a sign-in. Keyword tip: treat metrics as an observability tool, not an enforcement tool. Enforcement requires adaptive authentication.
Case-sensitive user pools

Explanation

Incorrect. Case-sensitive user pools control whether Amazon Cognito treats letter case as significant in usernames and email addresses during sign-in. This setting has no connection to threat detection or risk-based responses. Keyword tip: link this feature only to username and email string matching, never to risk evaluation or security enforcement.
Your answer is incorrect
Multi-factor authentication (MFA)

Explanation

Incorrect. MFA makes users provide a second authentication factor. MFA does not evaluate risk. MFA does not block a sign-in attempt automatically based on risk level. To block sign-ins automatically based on risk, Larkspur Robotics must configure adaptive authentication with a Block response for the target risk level. Keyword tip: MFA only adds a challenge step. MFA does not calculate or react to a risk score.
Correct answer
Adaptive authentication

Explanation

Correct. Adaptive authentication evaluates each sign-in attempt and assigns a risk score. The risk score is based on signals such as a new device, an unusual location, or a suspicious IP address. Larkspur Robotics can configure a response for each risk level, including Allow, Optional MFA, Require MFA, or Block. This lets the company automatically block sign-in attempts at an elevated risk level. Keyword tip: when a scenario describes automatically blocking or challenging sign-ins based on a calculated risk level, adaptive authentication is the feature being tested.

This question tests the difference between three Amazon Cognito capabilities: a static authentication factor (MFA), passive risk reporting (advanced security metrics), and automated risk-based response (adaptive authentication). Adaptive authentication is the correct choice whenever a requirement calls for dynamically allowing, challenging, or blocking sign-in attempts based on a calculated risk score. Advanced security metrics only send risk data to CloudWatch for visibility; the metrics do not take action on their own. MFA only adds a fixed second-factor step and does not respond to risk level at all. The key decision logic is to identify whether the requirement needs automated risk-driven action, passive reporting, or a fixed authentication step, and match that need to adaptive authentication, advanced security metrics, or MFA respectively.

Practical example: A K-12 software vendor like Larkspur Robotics lets students, teachers, and parents sign in to a shared portal from many different networks and devices, including school computers, home computers, and personal phones. To keep the portal open to legitimate users everywhere while still protecting student data, Larkspur Robotics configures adaptive authentication so that Amazon Cognito automatically blocks any sign-in attempt that scores as high risk, without requiring the company to build custom risk-detection logic.

Question 12Correct

Juniper Associates currently authenticates its fleet-tracking mobile application through Amazon Cognito user pools, with multi-factor authentication (MFA) enforced for every driver and dispatcher account. This application exposes sensitive data, including client shipment manifests and upcoming freight contract bids.

Given the sensitivity of this information, the logistics company now needs to notify its security team by email every time a user successfully logs in.

Which of the following would you recommend as the MOST optimal way of implementing this requirement within a short period of time?

Your answer is correct
Create an AWS Lambda function that uses Amazon Simple Email Service to send an email notification to the security team. Configure this function as an Amazon Cognito post-authentication Lambda trigger

Explanation

Correct. The post-authentication Lambda trigger runs immediately after a user successfully signs in. Amazon Cognito invokes this trigger only when authentication succeeds. Juniper Associates can attach a Lambda function to this trigger that sends an email through Amazon Simple Email Service to the security team. This approach directly satisfies the requirement to notify the security team after every successful login. Keyword tip: look for scenarios that need an action to happen right after a successful sign-in event — this is the signal for the post-authentication trigger.
Create an AWS Lambda function that uses Amazon Simple Email Service to send an email notification to the security team. Configure this function as an Amazon Cognito pre-authentication Lambda trigger

Explanation

Incorrect. The pre-authentication Lambda trigger runs before Amazon Cognito validates a sign-in attempt. Cognito uses this trigger to run custom logic that can accept or reject the sign-in attempt. This trigger does not run after a successful login, so it cannot notify the security team about completed login activity. Keyword tip: separate pre-authentication, which runs before sign-in completes and can block the attempt, from post-authentication, which runs after a successful sign-in and is ideal for notifications.
Configure an AWS Lambda function as a trigger to Amazon Cognito identity pools authenticated API operations. Create the Lambda function to utilize Amazon Simple Email Service to send an email notification to the security team

Explanation

Incorrect. Amazon Cognito identity pools provide temporary AWS credentials for authorization. Identity pools do not handle user authentication. Identity pools also do not support the same Lambda triggers, such as pre-authentication or post-authentication, that user pools support. Keyword tip: remember that identity pools control access to AWS resources, while user pools control sign-in and authentication.
Configure Amazon Cognito user pools authenticated API operations and MFA API operations to send all login data to Amazon Kinesis Data Streams. Configure an AWS Lambda function to analyze these streams and trigger an Amazon SNS notification to the security team based on user access

Explanation

Incorrect. This option describes a workflow where Amazon Cognito sends authentication data to Amazon Kinesis Data Streams. Amazon Cognito user pools do not natively stream login events to Kinesis Data Streams. This option links services together in a way that does not match any real AWS integration. Keyword tip: watch for answer choices that combine services without a documented native integration — these are usually invented distractors.

This question tests knowledge of Amazon Cognito user pool Lambda triggers and when each trigger runs during authentication. Use the pre-authentication trigger when custom logic must validate or block a sign-in attempt before it completes. Use the post-authentication trigger when custom logic must run after a successful sign-in, such as auditing, logging, or sending notifications. The correct decision depends on whether the required action must happen before or after authentication succeeds, and on distinguishing Cognito user pools, which handle authentication, from Cognito identity pools, which handle authorization.

Applied example: Juniper Associates can attach a Lambda function to the post-authentication trigger of its Cognito user pool. This function sends an email through Amazon Simple Email Service to the security team every time a driver or dispatcher signs in successfully. This setup gives the security team real-time visibility into login activity for an application that stores sensitive shipment and contract data, without requiring any change to the mobile application itself.

Question 13Incorrect

A recent internal audit found that a flagship crop-yield prediction application was often deployed with outdated code, because engineers had to manually trigger the deployment pipeline after each source code change and sometimes forgot to do so. Yellowpine Solutions, the agricultural technology company that owns the application, wants to build and deploy the application automatically as soon as any change is made to the source code.

As a Developer Associate, which of the following options would you suggest to trigger the deployment? (Select TWO.)

Keep the source code in an Amazon EBS volume and start AWS CodePipeline whenever there are updates to the source code

Explanation

Incorrect. Amazon EBS is block storage attached to a single EC2 instance. Amazon EBS is not a supported or practical source provider for AWS CodePipeline, and there is no built-in change-detection integration between EBS and CodePipeline. Keyword tip: EBS is instance-attached block storage, not a pipeline source repository, so it should never be chosen as a CodePipeline trigger mechanism.
Correct selection
Keep the source code in an Amazon S3 bucket and start AWS CodePipeline whenever a file in the S3 bucket is updated

Explanation

Correct. Amazon S3 is a supported source provider for AWS CodePipeline. When a pipeline uses an S3 bucket as its source, CodePipeline automatically creates an Amazon EventBridge rule. This rule starts the pipeline as soon as an object in the bucket changes. This gives Yellowpine Solutions a near real-time, event-driven deployment process instead of a manual one. Keyword tip: S3 combined with an event-driven trigger through EventBridge is the recommended change-detection method for CodePipeline.
Your selection is correct
Keep the source code in an AWS CodeCommit repository and start AWS CodePipeline whenever a change is pushed to the CodeCommit repository

Explanation

Correct. AWS CodeCommit is a fully supported source provider for AWS CodePipeline. When a pipeline uses a CodeCommit repository as its source, CodePipeline automatically creates an Amazon EventBridge rule. This rule starts the pipeline as soon as a change is pushed to the repository, giving Yellowpine Solutions an automatic, event-driven build and deployment process. Keyword tip: a CodeCommit push event triggering CodePipeline through EventBridge is the standard pattern for source-code-driven CI/CD.
Keep the source code in an Amazon S3 bucket and set up AWS CodePipeline to recur at an interval of every 15 minutes

Explanation

Incorrect. Polling an S3 bucket at a fixed interval, such as every 15 minutes, is an older change-detection method. This method adds delay compared to event-driven triggers, and AWS recommends disabling periodic checks in favor of an EventBridge rule. Keyword tip: a fixed polling interval, like 15 minutes, is a signal of an inefficient, non-recommended trigger method.
Your selection is incorrect
Keep the source code in Amazon EFS and start AWS CodePipeline whenever a file is updated

Explanation

Incorrect. Amazon EFS is not a supported source provider for AWS CodePipeline. There is no built-in mechanism that lets CodePipeline detect changes to files stored in an EFS file system. Keyword tip: only Amazon S3, AWS CodeCommit, and certain supported third-party repositories, such as GitHub, can act as CodePipeline source stages.

This question tests knowledge of which source providers AWS CodePipeline supports and how a pipeline can start automatically after a source code change. AWS CodePipeline natively supports Amazon S3 and AWS CodeCommit, as well as certain third-party providers like GitHub, as source stages. The recommended change-detection method for these sources is an Amazon EventBridge rule that starts the pipeline immediately when a change happens, instead of relying on periodic polling, which adds delay. Amazon EFS and Amazon EBS are not valid CodePipeline source providers, because they are file and block storage services without a built-in pipeline-trigger integration, so they cannot be used to detect source code changes automatically.

Real-world example: An agricultural technology company like Yellowpine Solutions relies on frequent, timely updates to its crop-yield prediction models to support farmers during planting and harvest seasons. By storing the application source code in AWS CodeCommit and letting an Amazon EventBridge rule start AWS CodePipeline on every push, the engineering team removes the manual trigger step that previously caused outdated deployments, and new model improvements reach production automatically and without delay.

Question 14Correct

Palisade Agency needs to scan an entire Amazon DynamoDB table without disrupting the live booking traffic of its hotel chain. The table, named PalisadeAgency-Reservations, is 45 GB in size and is provisioned with 8,000 read capacity units (RCUs) per second.

The scan must run during non-peak hours, when normal booking traffic consumes around 4,000 RCUs, and it must finish in the shortest possible time while the normal workload remains unaffected.

How would the Developer optimize this scan cost-effectively?

Use sequential scans and set the ConsistentRead parameter to false

Explanation

Incorrect. Setting ConsistentRead to false changes the scan from strongly consistent reads to eventually consistent reads. This change lowers the RCU cost of each read. This change does not split the scan into segments. This change does not make the scan finish faster or protect the normal workload's throughput. Keyword tip: eventually consistent reads lower RCU cost per request, but they do not parallelize or rate-limit a scan.
Your answer is correct
Use the Parallel Scan API operation and limit the rate

Explanation

Correct. The Parallel Scan API operation splits the table into multiple logical segments. Each segment can be scanned at the same time by a separate worker thread or process. This approach lets the Developer use the available spare RCUs and finish the scan much faster than a sequential scan would. Adding a rate limiter, such as the DynamoDB rate-limited scan utility, keeps the scan's RCU consumption inside the unused capacity, which protects the normal booking workload. Keyword tip: phrases like "scan a large table fast without impacting production traffic" point to Parallel Scan combined with rate limiting.
Use sequential scans and apply a FilterExpression

Explanation

Incorrect. A FilterExpression runs after DynamoDB reads the items from the table. A FilterExpression removes unwanted items from the results before they reach the client. A FilterExpression does not reduce the number of items read or the RCUs consumed. A FilterExpression does not make the scan faster and does not protect other workloads. Keyword tip: a FilterExpression shapes the output data, not the throughput consumption or the scan speed.
Increase read capacity units during the scan operation

Explanation

Incorrect. The table already has unused capacity during non-peak hours. 4,000 of the 8,000 provisioned RCUs are free at this time. Increasing capacity further adds cost without solving the real problem. The real problem is using the existing spare capacity efficiently, not adding more of it. Keyword tip: when a question says "cost-effectively" and spare capacity already exists, adding more capacity is rarely the correct choice.

This question tests the ability to scan a large DynamoDB table quickly without disrupting other workloads that share the same provisioned throughput. The Parallel Scan API operation divides a table into segments and scans them at the same time. Scanning segments at the same time uses idle capacity and finishes the scan faster than a sequential scan. A rate limiter must accompany the parallel scan so the scan does not consume more RCUs than are actually free, which would throttle or slow down normal application traffic. Sequential scans, changing the consistency model, or applying a FilterExpression can lower cost or shape the returned data, but none of these approaches increase scan speed or use idle capacity the way parallel scan does.

Use case: A hotel chain like Palisade Agency might need to run a nightly full-table scan across its reservation data to generate occupancy reports for the next day. Running this scan with the Parallel Scan API operation, combined with a rate limiter, lets Palisade Agency finish the report generation before guests start checking in, without slowing down the live booking system that shares the same DynamoDB table capacity.

Question 15Incorrect

Novapoint Technologies, a mining and minerals company, operates a fleet of automated ore-sorting machines across its extraction sites. The company uses an AWS Lambda function to run real-time image-analysis algorithms that classify mineral samples from sensor data, and this function is highly CPU-intensive due to the complexity of the image-processing calculations.

The engineering team now needs to reduce the average runtime of this function without rewriting its underlying code.

Which of the following approaches should be recommended to achieve this goal?

Correct answer
Deploy the function with its memory allocation set to the maximum amount

Explanation

Correct. Lambda allocates CPU power in proportion to the memory configured for a function. Increasing the memory setting proportionally increases the vCPU capacity available to the function. Lambda memory can scale up to 10 GB, which is the maximum configurable amount. This higher CPU capacity reduces runtime for CPU-intensive workloads, such as image-processing calculations. Keyword tip: for compute-heavy Lambda functions, increasing the memory setting is the primary way to increase effective CPU performance.
Your answer is incorrect
Deploy the function using Lambda layers

Explanation

Incorrect. Lambda layers are .zip archives that let a developer share code, custom runtimes, libraries, or configuration files across multiple functions. Layers help with code reuse and separation of concerns. Layers do not change the amount of CPU or memory allocated to a function's execution environment. Keyword tip: layers solve code organization and reuse problems, not performance or runtime problems.
Deploy the function with its CPU allocation set to the maximum amount

Explanation

Incorrect. AWS Lambda does not provide a setting that lets a developer configure CPU power directly. Lambda allocates CPU power automatically. Lambda calculates this allocation based on the memory setting of the function. A developer cannot configure CPU power as an independent setting. Keyword tip: if an option claims a Lambda function lets you set CPU directly, treat that option as invalid, because Lambda always ties compute power to the memory setting.
Deploy the function into multiple AWS Regions

Explanation

Incorrect. Deploying a Lambda function into multiple AWS Regions places copies of the function closer to end users in different geographic locations. This deployment pattern reduces latency and improves resilience. This deployment pattern does not change the compute capacity or CPU performance available to any single function invocation. Keyword tip: multi-Region deployment is a resilience and latency strategy, not a compute optimization technique.

This question tests understanding of how AWS Lambda allocates compute resources to a function. Lambda does not let a developer set CPU power directly. Lambda scales CPU power automatically and proportionally based on the memory setting configured for the function. A developer should increase the memory setting when a function is CPU-intensive and the runtime needs to decrease. A developer should use Lambda layers to share code or libraries across functions, not to improve performance. A developer should use multi-Region deployment to reduce latency for distributed users or to support disaster recovery, not to speed up a single function invocation. The core decision logic is recognizing that in the Lambda execution model, memory and CPU power are linked, so increasing memory is the actual lever for improving compute performance.

Use case: Novapoint Technologies runs an image-analysis function that classifies mineral samples from sensor data at its mining sites, and this function performs heavy computational work on each invocation. By increasing the memory allocation of this function, Novapoint Technologies increases the available CPU capacity for each invocation, which reduces the average processing time for each sample without requiring any changes to the function's code. This approach lets the company process ore-sorting data faster and keep pace with the throughput of its automated sorting machines.

A recent internal audit at an education technology company flagged a compliance risk: automated logs generated by a serverless grading platform might unintentionally capture student personal information. The audit was triggered after a data-privacy review of Orchardvale Systems' AWS Lambda-based assignment-scoring service, which streams runtime diagnostics to Amazon CloudWatch Logs.

Orchardvale Systems needs a way to guarantee that no personally identifiable information (PII) about students ends up persisted within those log streams.

What strategy should the developer adopt to meet this requirement?

Incorporate AWS X-Ray and configure it to filter out sensitive PII before logging.

Explanation

Incorrect. AWS X-Ray is a distributed tracing service. AWS X-Ray analyzes application performance and request flow. AWS X-Ray does not inspect, filter, or mask content written to CloudWatch Logs. Keyword tip: X-Ray relates to tracing and latency analysis, not log content sanitization.
Correct answer
Configure Amazon CloudWatch Logs data protection to detect and mask PII in log events (using managed data identifiers) before the data is stored.

Explanation

Correct. CloudWatch Logs data protection policies use managed data identifiers to automatically detect common categories of sensitive data, including PII such as names, addresses, and financial information, inside log events. CloudWatch Logs data protection then masks that sensitive data before CloudWatch Logs stores the log event. This feature works even if the application code accidentally writes sensitive values to the log. Keyword tip: the phrase "data protection policy" together with "managed data identifiers" in CloudWatch Logs points to this native detect-and-mask capability.
Manually insert logging commands into the application code while ensuring PII is not included.

Explanation

Incorrect. Relying only on careful coding practices depends on developers never making a mistake. This approach has no automated, AWS-managed layer to catch PII that a developer accidentally logs. Keyword tip: an option that depends only on manual code discipline, without a managed AWS control, is a weaker choice for exam questions about preventing accidental data exposure.
Your answer is incorrect
Implement AWS Secrets Manager for secure logging of sensitive information.

Explanation

Incorrect. AWS Secrets Manager stores, retrieves, and rotates secrets such as database credentials and API keys. AWS Secrets Manager does not scan or mask sensitive data inside application log output. Keyword tip: if an option describes rotating or retrieving credentials instead of scanning log content, that option does not solve log-based PII exposure.

This question tests knowledge of CloudWatch Logs data protection, a native feature that uses managed data identifiers to automatically detect and mask sensitive data types, including PII, inside log events before CloudWatch Logs stores them. Use CloudWatch Logs data protection when you need an AWS-managed, policy-driven safeguard instead of relying only on developer discipline. AWS Secrets Manager solves a different problem: it stores and rotates credentials, but it does not inspect log content. AWS X-Ray solves another different problem: it traces request flow and performance, but it also does not inspect or redact log content. The decision logic is to match the stated goal, which is preventing sensitive data from persisting in logs, to the AWS feature built specifically for that function, rather than picking a service that only manages secrets or only provides tracing.

In practice: an education technology company like Orchardvale Systems processes large volumes of student PII through Lambda functions that handle grading, enrollment, and progress tracking. If a developer accidentally logs a student's full name or email address during debugging, CloudWatch Logs data protection can automatically mask that value before it is stored, which helps Orchardvale Systems meet student-data privacy obligations without requiring every developer to manually audit every log statement.

Question 17Incorrect

A recent internal audit of observability coverage found that no trace data was appearing in AWS X-Ray, even though the AWS X-Ray SDK had been bundled into every AWS Lambda function used by Ridgeline Global, a maritime shipping company, to record outgoing calls for tracing purposes. When the team lead at Ridgeline Global opens the X-Ray service in the AWS Management Console to review the collected trace data, no data is available.

What is the most likely reason for this issue?

Correct answer
Fix the IAM role

Explanation

Correct. The Lambda execution role must include specific permissions, such as xray:PutTraceSegments and xray:PutTelemetryRecords, for the function to send trace data to the X-Ray service. Without these permissions, the X-Ray SDK cannot publish any data. The console will show no trace data even though tracing is enabled in the code. Keyword tip: when a fully instrumented service produces zero X-Ray data, check IAM permissions on the execution role first, because missing write permissions silently block trace delivery.
X-Ray only works with AWS Lambda aliases

Explanation

Incorrect. This statement is false. A Lambda alias is a pointer to a specific published version of a Lambda function, and an alias has no special relationship with X-Ray tracing. The X-Ray SDK must be bundled with the function code for every version, regardless of whether an alias is used. Keyword tip: aliases relate to Lambda versioning and traffic shifting, not to instrumentation or tracing capability.
Your answer is incorrect
Change the security group rules

Explanation

Incorrect. Security groups control network traffic to and from resources such as EC2 instances or VPC-attached Lambda functions. Access to the X-Ray API for publishing trace segments is controlled by IAM permissions, not by security group rules. Keyword tip: when an AWS service API call fails due to permissions rather than network connectivity, check IAM policies instead of security groups.
Enable X-Ray sampling

Explanation

Incorrect. Sampling controls what percentage of requests get traced. Sampling reduces cost and data volume, but it does not control whether the trace pipeline can deliver data at all. If IAM permissions are missing, no sampling configuration will produce visible trace data. Keyword tip: sampling problems usually cause partial or reduced data, not a complete absence of traces.

AWS X-Ray needs two things to deliver trace data: the X-Ray SDK bundled into the function code, and IAM permissions that grant the compute resource rights such as xray:PutTraceSegments and xray:PutTelemetryRecords. If instrumentation looks correct but no trace data shows up in the console, missing IAM permissions is the most common root cause. Sampling rules control the volume and rate of traces collected, but sampling only matters after the underlying permissions already work. Security groups are irrelevant to X-Ray API calls, because security groups only control network-level traffic, not service-level authorization; when data is missing entirely, check IAM permissions before checking sampling rates or network rules.

A similar situation: Ridgeline Global instruments its Lambda-based container-tracking functions with the X-Ray SDK to trace calls between its shipment-scheduling service and a third-party customs API, but a Terraform update accidentally strips the xray:PutTraceSegments permission from the execution role during a routine deployment. The X-Ray console shows no trace data at all, even though the SDK is present in the deployed code, and the fix is to restore the missing IAM permissions on the execution role rather than adjust sampling settings or network rules.

Question 18Incorrect

Decoupling user authentication from application logic is required so that Amazon EC2 instances running behind an Application Load Balancer can focus solely on business logic. Cascade Trust, a petrochemical company, operates this EC2 fleet to power an internal inspection-photo application used by field engineers, with traffic fronted by an Amazon CloudFront distribution for global content delivery.

Which of the following solutions addresses this requirement with minimal development effort?

Use Cognito Authentication via Cognito User Pools for your CloudFront distribution

Explanation

Incorrect. Amazon CloudFront does not natively integrate with Cognito User Pools for authentication. Adding this authentication to CloudFront requires building and maintaining a separate Lambda@Edge function that intercepts every request and validates tokens. This custom development work contradicts the requirement for minimal development effort. Keyword tip: CloudFront paired with Cognito User Pools always implies a custom Lambda@Edge solution, which needs more effort than the built-in Application Load Balancer integration.
Correct answer
Use Cognito Authentication via Cognito User Pools for your Application Load Balancer

Explanation

Correct. An Application Load Balancer supports a built-in authenticate action on HTTPS listener rules that integrates natively with Amazon Cognito User Pools. Cognito User Pools can authenticate users through social identity providers, SAML, LDAP, or Microsoft AD, without requiring custom code on the application servers. This setup offloads authentication to the load balancer, so application servers focus only on business logic, matching the minimal development effort requirement. Keyword tip: when a question mentions the ALB authenticate action or built-in authentication offload, the correct choice is Cognito User Pools attached to the ALB listener.
Use Cognito Authentication via Cognito Identity Pools for your Application Load Balancer

Explanation

Incorrect. Cognito Identity Pools provide temporary AWS credentials. Cognito Identity Pools do not perform user authentication. An Application Load Balancer listener rule cannot use a Cognito Identity Pool as its authentication mechanism. Keyword tip: the Application Load Balancer's built-in authenticate-cognito action only works with Cognito User Pools, not Cognito Identity Pools.
Your answer is incorrect
Use Cognito Authentication via Cognito Identity Pools for your CloudFront distribution

Explanation

Incorrect. Amazon Cognito Identity Pools do not authenticate application users. Cognito Identity Pools issue temporary AWS credentials to users who are already authenticated, or to guest users. Amazon CloudFront has no native way to attach a Cognito Identity Pool for authenticating application users. Keyword tip: when a question asks about authenticating application users, choose Cognito User Pools, not Cognito Identity Pools.

This question tests the difference between Amazon Cognito User Pools and Cognito Identity Pools, and which AWS services integrate natively with each. Cognito User Pools authenticate end users and issue identity tokens. Cognito Identity Pools exchange those tokens, or guest access, for temporary AWS credentials to access AWS resources. Use Cognito User Pools attached directly to an Application Load Balancer's HTTPS listener when the goal is to offload user authentication with minimal custom code, and use Cognito User Pools with CloudFront only if a custom Lambda@Edge function is acceptable, since CloudFront has no native Cognito integration.

Practical example: Cascade Trust, a petrochemical company, could use this pattern to protect an internal inspection-photo application used by field engineers. By attaching Cognito User Pools authentication directly to the Application Load Balancer listener, Cascade Trust ensures that only authenticated employees can upload or view inspection photos, without adding authentication code to the EC2 application servers. This lets the development team focus on business logic, such as processing and tagging inspection images, while the load balancer handles identity verification.
