Question 36Correct

After a routine performance audit revealed several booking-page timeouts during peak embarkation season, the operations team flagged the issue for immediate remediation. Westfield Union, a cruise line operator, runs a business-critical booking application on an Amazon EC2 instance, and the latest update is currently in the testing phase. The company wants a solution that tracks the average response time of the application and sends a notification to the manager whenever the response time exceeds a specific threshold.

The update will eventually be promoted to the production environment, where the solution will need to run across multiple EC2 instances. Which of the following options would Westfield Union combine to address these requirements? (Select TWO.)

Install and configure AWS Systems Manager Agent (SSM Agent) on the EC2 instances to monitor the response time and send the data to Amazon CloudWatch as a custom metric

Explanation

Incorrect. AWS Systems Manager Agent (SSM Agent) lets AWS Systems Manager manage, configure, and update EC2 instances, edge devices, on-premises servers, and virtual machines. SSM Agent does not collect application response-time data. SSM Agent also does not send custom metrics to CloudWatch. AWS Systems Manager can help automate the installation of the CloudWatch agent, but SSM Agent itself does not perform metric collection. Keyword tip: SSM Agent means instance management and automation, not metric or log collection.
Configure the application to write the response time to a log file on the instance. Install and configure the Amazon Inspector agent on the EC2 instances to read the logs and send the response time to Amazon EventBridge

Explanation

Incorrect. Amazon Inspector is an automated vulnerability management service. Amazon Inspector scans Amazon EC2 instances, AWS Lambda functions, and container workloads for software vulnerabilities and unintended network exposure. Amazon Inspector does not read application log files. Amazon Inspector also does not forward metrics to Amazon EventBridge. Keyword tip: Amazon Inspector means vulnerability and security scanning — do not confuse Amazon Inspector with a log or metrics collection agent.
Your selection is correct
Configure the application to write the response time to a log file on the EC2 instance. Install and configure the Amazon CloudWatch agent on the EC2 instance to stream the application logs to CloudWatch Logs. Create a metric filter for the response time from the log file

Explanation

Correct. The unified CloudWatch agent can collect log files from an EC2 instance and stream them to CloudWatch Logs. The application writes the response time to a log file. A CloudWatch Logs metric filter then extracts the response time value from that log file and turns it into a custom CloudWatch metric. This custom metric feeds the CloudWatch alarm from option 1. This approach also scales cleanly to multiple EC2 instances in production, because each instance runs its own CloudWatch agent and reports to the same metric namespace. Keyword tip: the phrase "log file plus metric filter" signals the standard pattern for turning application logs into a custom CloudWatch metric.
Configure an EventBridge custom rule to send an Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) notification when the average of the response time metric exceeds the threshold

Explanation

Incorrect. Amazon EventBridge can react to a CloudWatch alarm state change through an EventBridge rule that matches the alarm event. EventBridge can then invoke a target after that state change. However, EventBridge does not directly evaluate a metric average against a threshold. That threshold evaluation logic belongs to CloudWatch alarms, not EventBridge rules. Adding EventBridge as an extra step here creates unnecessary complexity, because a CloudWatch alarm can already publish directly to Amazon SNS. Keyword tip: EventBridge reacts to alarm state changes after the fact; EventBridge does not itself evaluate metric thresholds.
Your selection is correct
Create a CloudWatch alarm to send an Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) notification when the average of the response time metric exceeds the threshold

Explanation

Correct. A CloudWatch alarm watches a single metric or a math expression over one or more evaluation periods. When the metric crosses the threshold, the alarm state changes to ALARM. The alarm can then trigger an action, such as publishing a message to an Amazon SNS topic. This SNS notification is what alerts the manager. Keyword tip: look for the phrase "threshold breach triggers a notification" — this maps to a CloudWatch alarm paired with an SNS action.

This question tests the pattern for turning application-level data into a custom CloudWatch metric and then alerting on that metric. The correct pipeline has three parts: the application writes the response time to a log file, the CloudWatch agent streams that log file to CloudWatch Logs, and a CloudWatch Logs metric filter extracts the response time value and publishes it as a custom metric. A CloudWatch alarm then watches this custom metric and triggers an Amazon SNS notification when the metric crosses the threshold. Other AWS services solve different problems: SSM Agent manages and configures instances, Amazon Inspector scans for vulnerabilities, and EventBridge rules route events after a state change — none of these services can collect or evaluate a custom application metric on their own.

Use case: Westfield Union, a cruise line operator, could apply this exact pattern to its onboard booking application. During peak booking periods across multiple ships, the operations team needs an early warning when response times degrade, so that they can act before customers experience failed bookings. By deploying the CloudWatch agent and a metric filter on every EC2 instance behind the load balancer, and pairing that with a CloudWatch alarm and Amazon SNS notification, the team receives an immediate alert whenever performance drops below the defined service level, regardless of how many EC2 instances are running in production.

Question 37Incorrect

Driftline Guild, a museum and cultural heritage foundation, currently operates a single-Region order and archive-submission API that member museums use to catalog digital preservation records. As Driftline Guild prepares to expand its digital preservation program internationally, it must perform geographic load testing of this API by deploying resources to multiple AWS Regions.

How can Driftline Guild meet this requirement without additional application code?

Set up an AWS Organizations template that defines the load test resources across the organization. Leverage the AWS CLI create-stack-set command to create a stack set in the desired Regions

Explanation

Incorrect. AWS Organizations is an account management and governance service. Organizations helps you consolidate and centrally manage multiple AWS accounts. Organizations does not let you author templates that define or provision infrastructure resources, such as load test environments. This option mixes a valid mechanism, stack sets, with an invalid template source. Keyword tip: if a service description involves defining infrastructure but the service's real purpose is account governance, that service is the wrong tool for provisioning resources.
Your answer is incorrect
Set up an AWS CloudFormation template that defines the load test resources. Develop region-specific AWS Lambda functions to create a stack from the AWS CloudFormation template in each Region when the respective function is invoked

Explanation

Incorrect. This approach requires developing and maintaining region-specific AWS Lambda functions. Each function triggers stack creation in its own Region. Writing these functions counts as additional application code. CloudFormation StackSets already performs this same task natively through a single CLI command, without any custom code. Keyword tip: if a proposed solution requires writing custom Lambda functions to replicate infrastructure across Regions, that solution is over-engineered compared to using StackSets directly.
Correct answer
Set up an AWS CloudFormation template that defines the load test resources. Leverage the AWS CLI create-stack-set command to create a stack set in the desired Regions

Explanation

Correct. AWS CloudFormation StackSets extends a single CloudFormation stack. StackSets let you create, update, or delete stacks across multiple accounts and multiple AWS Regions with one operation. StackSets use a single template as the source of truth for every target Region. This approach meets the requirement to deploy the same load test resources to multiple Regions without writing any additional application code. Keyword tip: when a scenario asks for deploying identical infrastructure across multiple accounts or Regions using one template and one operation, choose AWS CloudFormation StackSets.
Set up an AWS Cloud Development Kit (CDK) Toolkit that defines the load test resources. Leverage the CDK CLI to create a stack from the template in each Region

Explanation

Incorrect. The AWS Cloud Development Kit (CDK) is a framework for defining infrastructure as code. CDK code synthesizes into AWS CloudFormation templates. The CDK CLI deploys one stack per invocation. CDK does not natively provide multi-Region or multi-account orchestration in a single operation the way StackSets does. Using CDK for this requirement would need additional scripting or looping logic across Regions, which is extra code. Keyword tip: CDK is for authoring infrastructure as code, but multi-Region or multi-account fan-out at deployment time is the specific job of CloudFormation StackSets.

AWS CloudFormation StackSets extends standard CloudFormation stacks so a single template can provision, update, or delete resources across multiple AWS accounts and multiple Regions in one operation. Use StackSets when you need consistent, repeatable infrastructure deployed to many Regions without writing custom orchestration code. Use CDK on its own only when you need custom per-Region logic that StackSets cannot express, since CDK deploys one stack per invocation and does not fan out across Regions automatically. Avoid AWS Organizations for actual resource provisioning, because Organizations is strictly an account governance service and cannot author or deploy infrastructure templates.

Business scenario: Driftline Guild's cataloging API must handle traffic from member museums located in different geographic regions once its international preservation program launches. By defining the load test resources in one CloudFormation template and deploying them through a stack set, Driftline Guild's engineering team can simulate realistic multi-Region traffic patterns without maintaining separate deployment scripts or custom Lambda triggers for each Region.

Question 38Correct

A web application requires improved read performance for highly requested user profile data that currently resides in Amazon RDS. Sablecrest Networks, a book and media publisher, is developing this application, which lets readers follow other users and favorite authors. Some user profiles are requested far more often than others, so a developer recommends introducing Amazon ElastiCache as a caching layer to reduce the load on the database.

The entire user dataset cannot fit into ElastiCache without incurring significant costs, so only the most frequently requested profiles should be cached. Because Sablecrest Networks' platform handles high traffic, cached profile data can be stale for a short period, as long as it is no more than one minute old.

Which caching strategy should be implemented to meet these requirements?

Use a Write Through strategy without TTL

Explanation

Incorrect. A Write Through strategy writes every record to the cache each time the database is updated. This means the cache would need to hold the entire dataset to stay consistent. That defeats the goal of caching only the most popular profiles. Without a TTL, stale entries would never expire. Keyword tip: Write Through populates the cache on every write, so it does not work well when the dataset is too large to fully cache.
Use a Write Through strategy with TTL

Explanation

Incorrect. A Write Through strategy with a TTL still writes every updated record into the cache, regardless of how often that record is read. This fills the cache with rarely requested profiles, which exceeds the available cache capacity and budget. Keyword tip: Write Through fits scenarios where nearly all data must stay in the cache and remain consistent, not scenarios where only a small hot subset should be cached.
Your answer is correct
Use a Lazy Loading strategy with TTL

Explanation

Correct. Lazy Loading, also called cache-aside, loads data into ElastiCache only when the application requests it and finds a cache miss. This naturally results in caching only the most popular user profiles, which keeps costs low. Adding a TTL of one minute makes each cached entry expire after one minute, forcing the application to reload fresh data from Amazon RDS. This TTL satisfies the requirement that cached data must never be more than one minute old. Keyword tip: Lazy Loading combined with a TTL is the standard pattern for caching a hot subset of data while keeping staleness within a defined limit.
Use a Lazy Loading strategy without TTL

Explanation

Incorrect. Lazy Loading correctly caches only the profiles that are frequently requested. Without a TTL, cached entries never expire. This means stale data could remain in the cache indefinitely, which violates the one-minute staleness requirement. Keyword tip: whenever a scenario states a maximum staleness window, a TTL is required no matter which loading strategy is used.

This question tests the choice between two core ElastiCache caching strategies, Lazy Loading (cache-aside) and Write Through, and when to add a Time To Live (TTL) value to cached entries. Lazy Loading only loads a record into the cache after the application reads it and finds a cache miss, so it naturally caches only the records that are actually requested, which fits scenarios where just a subset of data needs to stay cached. Write Through writes every updated record into the cache at the same time it writes to the database, so the cache stays fully synchronized, which fits scenarios where nearly all records must remain available in the cache. A TTL should be added whenever the scenario states a maximum allowed staleness, because a TTL forces the cache to expire old entries and reload fresh data from the source of truth.

Business scenario: Sablecrest Networks operates a social reading platform where popular authors and influencers receive many more profile views than average users. Caching only the most frequently requested profiles keeps ElastiCache costs low while still reducing repeated reads from Amazon RDS for the busiest accounts. Setting a one-minute TTL on each cached profile lets Sablecrest Networks tolerate brief staleness in exchange for lower database load, without ever serving data that is meaningfully out of date.

Question 39Correct

Thornfield Labs, a construction and engineering firm, collects data from vibration sensors installed at active job sites. An AWS Lambda function stores the sensor data in an Amazon SQS Standard queue, and an Amazon EC2 instance processes the data and stores it in an Amazon Redshift data warehouse used for structural analytics.

A fault in the sensors' software is causing occasional duplicate messages to be sent. Timestamps on the duplicate messages show that they are generated within a few seconds of the primary message.

How can a developer prevent duplicate data from being stored in the data warehouse?

Send a ChangeMessageVisibility call with VisibilityTimeout set to 45 seconds after the receipt of every message from the queue

Explanation

Incorrect. A ChangeMessageVisibility call changes the visibility timeout for a message that a consumer has already received. This action hides the message from other consumers for a set period. It does not detect or remove duplicate messages that are already sitting in the queue. A duplicate message would still be processed as a separate message later. Keyword tip: visibility timeout controls how long a message stays hidden during processing, not whether duplicate content is removed.
Use a FIFO queue and configure the Lambda function to add a message group ID to the messages generated by each individual sensor

Explanation

Incorrect. A message group ID is a FIFO queue feature that preserves the order of related messages within the same group. This feature controls sequencing, not duplicate detection. Two identical messages placed in the same message group would still both be delivered and processed unless a separate deduplication mechanism is also used. Keyword tip: message group ID controls ordering; message deduplication ID or content-based deduplication controls duplicate suppression. These are two separate FIFO queue features.
Configure a redrive policy, specify a destination dead-letter queue, and set the maxReceiveCount to 1

Explanation

Incorrect. A redrive policy and a maxReceiveCount value control what happens when a message fails processing multiple times. After the maxReceiveCount is reached, Amazon SQS moves the message to a dead-letter queue. This feature handles processing failures. It does not stop duplicate messages from entering the queue in the first place. The duplicate sensor messages in this scenario are not processing failures. They are separate messages that arrive close together. Keyword tip: a redrive policy and a dead-letter queue solve processing failures, not duplicate delivery.
Your answer is correct
Use a FIFO queue and configure the Lambda function to add a message deduplication token to the message body

Explanation

Correct. Amazon SQS FIFO queues support exactly-once processing when combined with message deduplication. The Lambda function can add a message deduplication token to each message body, or the queue can use content-based deduplication instead. Amazon SQS then discards any duplicate message that arrives within the 5-minute deduplication interval. Only one copy of each sensor reading reaches the Amazon EC2 consumer and Amazon Redshift. Keyword tip: the phrase "message deduplication token" or "content-based deduplication" on a FIFO queue signals the standard mechanism for eliminating duplicate messages.

This question tests the difference between two separate Amazon SQS FIFO queue features: message group ID and message deduplication. Message group ID controls the order in which messages within the same group are processed. It does not detect or remove duplicate messages. Message deduplication, using either a deduplication token or content-based deduplication, removes duplicate messages that arrive within a 5-minute window. Use FIFO queues with deduplication whenever duplicate messages must not reach a downstream system. Use message group ID only when strict ordering within a logical group of messages matters. A redrive policy and dead-letter queue handle repeated processing failures, and ChangeMessageVisibility only changes how long a message stays hidden from other consumers; neither feature removes duplicate messages.

Use case: Thornfield Labs relies on accurate structural sensor readings to make safety decisions on active job sites. If duplicate vibration readings reached Amazon Redshift, the analytics team could see falsely amplified stress values and trigger unnecessary site shutdowns. Switching to a FIFO queue with message deduplication tokens ensures each sensor reading is stored exactly once, keeping the structural analytics data accurate.

Question 40Correct

Crestline Foundation must guarantee that any failed order in its equipment procurement pipeline can be debugged later and reprocessed without losing data. The organization, a weather and climate research agency that resupplies remote atmospheric monitoring stations, uses an Amazon SQS queue named CrestlineSensorOrders to queue replacement-sensor orders, and an AWS Lambda function processes each order from that queue.

The team has recently noticed that a significant number of orders are failing to process.

How can a developer MOST effectively manage these failures to debug the failed orders later and reprocess them, as necessary?

Log the failed orders from the CrestlineSensorOrders queue using Amazon CloudWatch Logs

Explanation

Incorrect. Amazon SQS does not automatically send failed message events to Amazon CloudWatch Logs. Amazon CloudWatch mainly provides metrics about queue behavior, such as message counts. Amazon CloudWatch does not store the content of a failed message. Keyword tip: Amazon CloudWatch Logs needs explicit application-level logging code and does not natively isolate failed SQS messages.
Publish failed orders from the CrestlineSensorOrders queue to an Amazon SNS topic

Explanation

Incorrect. Amazon SNS is a publish/subscribe notification service. Amazon SNS does not track how many times a message has failed processing in a queue. Amazon SNS has no built-in mechanism to isolate only the failed orders from the source queue. Keyword tip: Amazon SNS is for fanning out notifications to subscribers, not for isolating queue processing failures.
Send failed orders from the CrestlineSensorOrders queue to AWS CloudTrail logs

Explanation

Incorrect. AWS CloudTrail records API calls and account activity for auditing purposes. AWS CloudTrail does not record application-level message content. AWS CloudTrail cannot capture the body of a failed order message for later debugging. Keyword tip: connect AWS CloudTrail with API activity auditing, not with message payload inspection.
Your answer is correct
Implement a dead-letter queue for failed orders from the CrestlineSensorOrders queue

Explanation

Correct. A dead-letter queue (DLQ) is a separate queue that a source queue can target for messages that fail processing repeatedly. When a message exceeds the maxReceiveCount setting on the source queue, Amazon SQS moves that message to the dead-letter queue automatically. The dead-letter queue keeps the full message body, so a developer can inspect the failed order later and reprocess it. Keyword tip: when a question asks how to isolate and later reprocess failed SQS messages, think dead-letter queue.

Amazon SQS dead-letter queues (DLQs) exist to isolate messages that a consumer cannot process successfully after a set number of receive attempts. A DLQ preserves the full message body, so a developer can debug the failure later and reprocess the message without any data loss. Amazon CloudWatch Logs only captures what an application explicitly logs and does not track failed SQS messages on its own. AWS CloudTrail only records API calls and account activity, and Amazon SNS only fans out notifications; neither service tracks failed-message counts or isolates failed messages from a source queue. The decision logic is to match the requirement of preserving and later reprocessing failed message content with the AWS service purpose-built for that job, which is the SQS dead-letter queue.

Consider this scenario: Crestline Foundation depends on timely resupply of replacement sensors for its remote atmospheric monitoring stations, so a lost or unprocessed order can delay critical weather data collection. By configuring a dead-letter queue on the CrestlineSensorOrders queue, the operations team can review every failed order, identify the root cause, and safely retry the order without manually searching through logs or losing order details.

Question 41Correct

Dovetail Networks operates a music streaming platform that recently moved its internal job-notification queues from a self-hosted message broker cluster to Amazon SQS, using the queues to coordinate track-encoding tasks between microservices. The engineering team now wants to reduce the number of billable API requests generated when consumers poll these queues for new messages.

Which of the following options should be recommended to meet this requirement?

Your answer is correct
Use SQS long polling to retrieve messages from the Amazon SQS queues

Explanation

Correct. Long polling makes Amazon SQS wait for a message to arrive before sending a response, instead of responding right away when the queue is empty. The wait time can be set up to 20 seconds. This wait reduces the number of empty responses. Fewer empty responses mean fewer billable requests, so long polling lowers the cost of consuming messages. Keyword tip: when a scenario mentions reducing SQS costs or reducing empty responses, this points to long polling, configured through the ReceiveMessageWaitTimeSeconds setting.
Use SQS message timers to retrieve messages from the Amazon SQS queues

Explanation

Incorrect. A message timer delays how long a newly sent message stays hidden from consumers, from 0 seconds up to 15 minutes. A message timer only affects the moment a message becomes visible after it is sent. A message timer does not control how consumers retrieve messages, and a message timer does not reduce polling costs. Keyword tip: message timers control visibility delay at send time, not the retrieval or polling process.
Use SQS short polling to retrieve messages from the Amazon SQS queues

Explanation

Incorrect. Short polling is the default Amazon SQS behavior. With short polling, Amazon SQS returns a response immediately, even if no messages are available in the queue. Because responses return immediately and may be empty, consumers using short polling often send more requests overall, which increases cost. Keyword tip: short polling returns immediately and can raise costs through frequent empty receives.
Use SQS visibility timeout to retrieve messages from the Amazon SQS queues

Explanation

Incorrect. Visibility timeout controls how long a message stays hidden from other consumers after one consumer has already retrieved that message. Visibility timeout exists to prevent duplicate processing of the same message. Visibility timeout does not retrieve messages from the queue and does not reduce the number of polling requests. Keyword tip: visibility timeout is about preventing duplicate processing of in-flight messages, not about polling cost.

This question tests understanding of Amazon SQS polling behavior and how each polling mode affects request cost. Long polling should be used whenever the goal is to reduce the number of billable API calls, because it waits up to 20 seconds for a message to become available before responding, which cuts down on empty responses. Short polling returns immediately regardless of whether a message is available, which increases the number of requests a consumer must send and therefore increases cost. Visibility timeout and message timers are unrelated to retrieval polling: visibility timeout hides an in-flight message from other consumers, and a message timer delays when a newly sent message first becomes visible.

Consider this scenario: Dovetail Networks runs many worker processes that check an SQS queue for new track-encoding jobs throughout the day. If each worker uses short polling, the workers send a request every few seconds even when no jobs are waiting, and each of those requests is billed. By switching the workers to long polling with a wait time close to 20 seconds, Dovetail Networks reduces the number of requests sent during idle periods, which lowers the monthly SQS bill without changing how encoding jobs are processed.

References:

https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSSimpleQueueService/latest/SQSDeveloperGuide/sqs-short-and-long-polling.html

Question 42Incorrect

Confidential client case records at Fairmount Continental, a law firm, are currently stored in Amazon DynamoDB tables that rely on DynamoDB's default server-side encryption at rest. A new firm-wide data protection policy now requires that this sensitive data be encrypted before it is ever submitted to DynamoDB.

How can a developer meet this requirement?

Your answer is incorrect
Use the UpdateTable operation to switch to a customer managed customer master key (CMK).

Explanation

Incorrect. Switching to a customer managed CMK with UpdateTable changes who controls and rotates the encryption key, and it still only affects server-side encryption at rest. The data is still unencrypted plaintext when the application sends the data to DynamoDB. This does not meet a requirement for encryption before submission. Keyword tip: separate two ideas in these questions: who manages the encryption key (AWS managed CMK vs. customer managed CMK), and where the encryption happens (client-side vs. server-side). Only the second idea answers a "before submission" requirement.
Correct answer
Use the DynamoDB Encryption Client to enable end-to-end protection using client-side encryption.

Explanation

Correct. The DynamoDB Encryption Client is a client-side encryption library. A developer uses this library to encrypt sensitive data inside the application, before the data is sent to DynamoDB. This approach gives end-to-end protection, because the data is already encrypted when it leaves the application and stays encrypted until the application decrypts it again. Server-side encryption only protects data after DynamoDB receives it, so server-side encryption alone cannot meet a requirement that data be encrypted before submission. Keyword tip: when a requirement says data must be encrypted before it leaves the application or before submission to a service, that phrase points to a client-side encryption library, such as the DynamoDB Encryption Client.
Use the UpdateTable operation to switch to an AWS managed customer master key (CMK).

Explanation

Incorrect. Switching to an AWS managed customer master key (CMK) with the UpdateTable operation changes only the key used for DynamoDB's server-side encryption at rest. The data still travels to DynamoDB over an encrypted connection as plaintext content, and DynamoDB encrypts the data only after the data arrives. This does not satisfy a requirement that data be encrypted before submission. Keyword tip: the UpdateTable operation combined with CMK selection signals server-side encryption at rest, not encryption that happens before the data leaves the application.
Use AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) to create one certificate for each DynamoDB table.

Explanation

Incorrect. AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) provisions and manages SSL/TLS certificates. These certificates secure network connections. A certificate cannot be attached to a DynamoDB table to encrypt item data. ACM does not encrypt data before submission to DynamoDB. Keyword tip: if an option mentions ACM in the context of encrypting data before it reaches a database, treat it as a distractor, because ACM only protects data in transit over the network, not data content itself.

This question tests the difference between server-side encryption at rest and client-side encryption before transmission. Server-side encryption, whether it uses an AWS managed CMK or a customer managed CMK, protects data only after DynamoDB receives the data. The UpdateTable operation can switch between these two key types, but UpdateTable never encrypts data before submission. AWS Certificate Manager is unrelated to encrypting DynamoDB item data, because ACM only manages TLS certificates for network transport. When a requirement states that data must be encrypted before it leaves the application, only a client-side encryption library, such as the DynamoDB Encryption Client, satisfies that requirement, because this library encrypts each item locally before the application calls the DynamoDB API.

In practice: A law firm like Fairmount Continental may need to guarantee that no unencrypted client case data ever leaves its application servers, even briefly, in order to satisfy strict client confidentiality agreements. By integrating the DynamoDB Encryption Client into its application code, Fairmount Continental encrypts sensitive fields locally before each write operation. As a result, the data that travels over the network and the data stored in DynamoDB are already protected end-to-end.

Question 43Incorrect

Ironclad Global must guarantee that multiple groups of write actions applied to an Amazon DynamoDB table either all succeed or all fail together, with no partial updates, and must ensure that repeating the same operation does not cause duplicate changes. The company, a commercial real estate firm building a new serverless leasing application, needs to select the correct DynamoDB write approach.

Which solution will meet these requirements?

Correct answer
Update the items in the table using the TransactWriteItems operation to group the changes

Explanation

Correct. TransactWriteItems is a synchronous DynamoDB operation. TransactWriteItems groups up to 25 write actions across one or more tables in the same AWS account and Region into one all-or-nothing transaction. Either every action in the group succeeds, or none of the actions apply. TransactWriteItems also enforces idempotency using a client token, so retrying the same transaction does not create duplicate changes. Keyword tip: when a scenario mentions "all-or-nothing" or "atomic" writes across multiple DynamoDB items, choose TransactWriteItems.
Create an Amazon SQS FIFO queue and use the SendMessageBatch operation to group the changes

Explanation

Incorrect. Amazon SQS FIFO queues process messages exactly once and preserve message order. An SQS FIFO queue does not perform writes to DynamoDB. An SQS FIFO queue also does not enforce atomicity across DynamoDB write actions. The requirement asks for atomic, all-or-nothing writes to a DynamoDB table. This capability belongs to the DynamoDB API, not to a messaging service. Keyword tip: if a solution adds an external queueing service instead of using the database's own transactional API, treat it as a likely distractor for atomicity requirements.
Your answer is incorrect
Update the items in the table using the BatchWriteItem operation and configure idempotency at the table level

Explanation

Incorrect. BatchWriteItem does not guarantee all-or-nothing behavior. If some write actions in the batch fail, for example due to throttling, DynamoDB applies the successful actions and returns the failed actions for the caller to retry. DynamoDB has no table-level setting that makes BatchWriteItem behave as an atomic transaction. Keyword tip: BatchWriteItem improves write throughput, not atomicity, and any failed items require manual retry logic.
Enable DynamoDB Streams and capture new images. Update the items in the table using the BatchWriteItem operation

Explanation

Incorrect. DynamoDB Streams captures a time-ordered record of item-level changes. Developers use DynamoDB Streams to trigger AWS Lambda functions or to replicate data to other systems. DynamoDB Streams does not add atomicity or idempotency to a batch of write actions. Adding DynamoDB Streams on top of BatchWriteItem does not change how BatchWriteItem handles partial failures. Keyword tip: DynamoDB Streams supports change capture and downstream processing, not transactional guarantees.

This question tests the distinction between DynamoDB's transactional write API and its batch write API. Use TransactWriteItems when a scenario requires that multiple write actions across one or more items either all succeed or all fail together, and when the operation must also be idempotent on retry. Use BatchWriteItem when a scenario requires high write throughput and can tolerate partial failures that the application retries individually. DynamoDB Streams and Amazon SQS FIFO queues solve different problems entirely: DynamoDB Streams supports change capture for downstream processing, and SQS FIFO queues support ordered, exactly-once message delivery, but neither provides atomic write guarantees for a DynamoDB table.

In practice: a commercial real estate firm like Ironclad Global might update a property record, a lease record, and a tenant billing record together whenever a new lease is signed. If any one of these three updates fails, the firm needs all three updates to roll back together to avoid an inconsistent leasing record. TransactWriteItems lets the developer group these related updates into a single atomic operation, so partial or duplicate updates never reach the database.

Question 44Correct

Harborview Works needs to resolve a persistent API failure that is blocking a customer-facing loan application service before its next compliance audit. The company, a regional banking institution based in Denver, has configured a Lambda integration in Amazon API Gateway for its HarborviewWorks-LoanProcessor function using a stage variable.

However, every invocation of the API method returns an "Internal server error" message with a 500 status code.

What steps should the developer take to fix the issue?

Your answer is correct
If you create a stage variable to call a Lambda function through your API, you must add the required permissions. Update your Lambda function's resource-based AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) policy so that it grants invoke permission to API Gateway

Explanation

Correct. When API Gateway invokes a Lambda function through a stage variable, the Lambda function's resource-based IAM policy must explicitly grant invoke permission to API Gateway. When the API Gateway console builds a standard Lambda integration, it adds this permission automatically. When a developer uses a stage variable instead, the developer must add this permission manually, either directly on the resource-based policy or through an IAM role that API Gateway assumes. This missing permission is the documented root cause of the "Internal server error" with a 500 status code in Lambda integrations that use stage variables. Keyword tip: a 500 error combined with a stage variable and a Lambda integration points to a missing resource-based policy invoke permission.
API calls can't exceed the maximum allowed API request rate per account and per Region. Implement error retries and exponential backoffs to fix the error

Explanation

Incorrect. Exceeding the maximum API request rate produces a distinct "Rate Exceeded" throttling error, not an "Internal server error" with a 500 status code. Retries and exponential backoff are the correct response to throttling errors. Retries and exponential backoff do not fix a missing-permission integration failure like the one described in this scenario. Keyword tip: match the exact error message and status code to its root cause category before choosing a remediation.
When setting the Lambda function as the value of a stage variable, use the function's ARN and not the function alias for setting up the value

Explanation

Incorrect. AWS documentation states the opposite approach. When a developer sets a Lambda function as the value of a stage variable, the developer should use the function's local, unqualified name, optionally with an alias or version. API Gateway expands that value into the full ARN internally. Supplying a full ARN directly as the stage variable value is not the documented approach, and it does not address the permission issue that causes the 500 error. Keyword tip: stage variable values for Lambda integrations reference the function name or alias, not the ARN.
If you create a stage variable to call a function through your API, you must add the required permissions. Create an IAM role that your Lambda function can assume when invoking the respective AWS resources

Explanation

Incorrect. Creating an IAM role that the Lambda function assumes controls what the Lambda function can access when it calls other AWS resources. This role does not control whether API Gateway is allowed to invoke the Lambda function. The 500 error in this scenario happens because API Gateway lacks invoke permission on the Lambda function. The correct fix is to grant that invoke permission through the Lambda function's resource-based policy or through an IAM role that API Gateway assumes. Keyword tip: check the direction of the permission, meaning who is allowed to invoke whom, when troubleshooting Lambda and API Gateway integration errors.

This question tests the developer's understanding of Lambda-API Gateway integration permissions. When a developer selects a Lambda function through a stage variable instead of a direct integration, API Gateway does not automatically add the invoke permission on the Lambda function's resource-based policy. The developer must add that permission manually, either on the resource-based policy or through an IAM role that API Gateway assumes. The decision logic for troubleshooting a 500 "Internal server error" on a Lambda-backed API method is to check this permission first, rather than assuming the cause is throttling, ARN formatting, or the Lambda function's own outbound permissions to other AWS resources.

Consider this scenario: Harborview Works uses a single Lambda function across multiple API Gateway stages, such as development, staging, and production, by referencing the function through a stage variable, so each stage variable value points to a different alias of the same function. Because the console did not auto-generate the invoke permission for this stage-variable-based setup, the loan-processing API returns 500 errors until the developer manually attaches the resource-based policy statement, or an assumable IAM role, that grants apigateway.amazonaws.com permission to invoke the function.

https://docs.aws.amazon.com/apigateway/latest/developerguide/how-to-set-stage-variables-aws-console.html

Question 45Incorrect

To ensure trace data is reliably collected from its containerized backend services, Elmsworth Innovations—an online gaming company running latency-sensitive multiplayer services—needs to run the AWS X-Ray daemon alongside its Docker containers deployed using AWS Fargate on Amazon ECS.

What must the development team do to ensure this setup works correctly? (Select TWO.)

Deploy the X-Ray daemon agent as a process on the underlying EC2 instance

Explanation

Incorrect. AWS Fargate fully manages the underlying compute infrastructure. There is no EC2 instance that the development team can access. Because of this, the team cannot install or run the X-Ray daemon as a standalone process on a host. Keyword tip: if a question mentions Fargate, rule out any option that requires direct EC2 host access.
Your selection is incorrect
Deploy the X-Ray daemon agent as a daemon set on ECS

Explanation

Incorrect. A daemon set runs one copy of the X-Ray daemon on each host in a cluster. This pattern works for Amazon ECS on EC2, where hosts are visible and manageable. AWS Fargate does not expose the underlying host, so a daemon set cannot be used. Keyword tip: the term 'daemon set' implies host-level access, which Fargate does not provide.
Provide the correct IAM instance role to the underlying EC2 instance

Explanation

Incorrect. AWS Fargate removes the need to manage EC2 instances. There is no EC2 instance for the team to attach an instance role to. In Fargate, permissions are granted through IAM task roles instead of instance roles. Keyword tip: the term 'instance role' points to EC2 or ECS-on-EC2 patterns, not Fargate.
Your selection is correct
Provide the correct IAM task role to the X-Ray container

Explanation

Correct. Fargate tasks have no accessible EC2 instance, so permissions must be granted at the task level. The X-Ray daemon sidecar container needs an IAM task role with X-Ray permissions, such as xray:PutTraceSegments and xray:PutTelemetryRecords, to send trace data to the X-Ray service. Keyword tip: the term 'task role' (not 'instance role') is the correct IAM permission model for Fargate.
Correct selection
Deploy the X-Ray daemon agent as a sidecar container

Explanation

Correct. In AWS Fargate, the X-Ray daemon must be packaged as its own container image. This container is deployed as a sidecar within the same task definition as the application container. The task definition's port mappings and network mode allow the application container and the X-Ray sidecar container to communicate. Keyword tip: 'sidecar container' is the standard X-Ray daemon deployment pattern for Fargate tasks.

This question tests knowledge of how AWS X-Ray daemon deployment differs between Amazon ECS on EC2 and AWS Fargate. Fargate does not expose the underlying host, so the X-Ray daemon cannot run as an EC2 process or as a daemon set. Instead, the X-Ray daemon must be packaged as a container image and deployed as a sidecar container within the task definition, communicating with the application container through defined port mappings and the task's network mode. Permissions must also come from an IAM task role rather than an instance role, because Fargate tasks have no EC2 instance profile to attach permissions to.

In practice: An online gaming company like Elmsworth Innovations often runs many microservices in Fargate to support matchmaking, leaderboards, and session management with minimal operational overhead. To trace requests across these services and diagnose latency spikes during peak player activity, the team adds an X-Ray daemon sidecar to each task definition and grants it an IAM task role with X-Ray permissions, allowing full visibility into request flows without managing any EC2 hosts.

Question 46Correct

The data engineering team at Amberfield Cooperative, an environmental monitoring agency that tracks water quality sensor readings across regional rivers, is building an AWS Lambda function to process incoming sensor telemetry from an Amazon Kinesis Data Stream. Whenever the function fails to process a batch of sensor records, the team needs an automatic notification sent to on-call administrators so they can investigate before the failure affects compliance reporting.

How should the team configure the function to meet this requirement?

Push the failed records to an Amazon SQS queue

Explanation

Incorrect. An Amazon SQS queue can be configured as a Lambda Destination for failed invocations. Amazon SQS only stores the failure record in the queue for later processing. Amazon SQS does not send a notification to administrators by itself. Keyword tip: Amazon SQS supports decoupled asynchronous processing and retry, not direct human notification.
Your answer is correct
Configure an Amazon SNS topic as an on-failure destination

Explanation

Correct. AWS Lambda Destinations let a function route the execution record of an asynchronous invocation to a target resource without extra code inside the function. When an Amazon SNS topic is configured as the on-failure destination, Lambda automatically publishes the failure execution record, including the invocation payload and error details, to that SNS topic. Amazon SNS can then deliver the notification to administrators through email, SMS, or another subscription type. Keyword tip: the phrase "on-failure destination" combined with a requirement to notify people is a strong signal that Amazon SNS configured as a Lambda Destination is the correct answer.
Separate the Lambda handler from the core logic

Explanation

Incorrect. Separating the Lambda handler from the core logic is a code organization practice. This practice improves testability and maintainability of the function code. This practice does not create any mechanism for sending a notification when processing fails. Keyword tip: this pattern relates to unit testing and code structure, not to failure notification.
Use Amazon CloudWatch Events to send the processed data

Explanation

Incorrect. Amazon CloudWatch Events, now largely replaced by Amazon EventBridge, reacts to state changes and scheduled events. Amazon CloudWatch Events does not route the execution result of an asynchronous Lambda invocation by default. Sending a failure notification through CloudWatch Events would require additional event pattern configuration that is not part of this option. Keyword tip: CloudWatch Events and EventBridge rules trigger on event patterns, not automatically on Lambda invocation success or failure.

This question tests knowledge of AWS Lambda Destinations. Lambda Destinations let an asynchronous invocation route its execution result, either success or failure, to a target resource such as another Lambda function, Amazon SNS, Amazon SQS, or Amazon EventBridge, without requiring custom code inside the function. When the requirement is to alert administrators about a failure, Amazon SNS is the correct on-failure destination because Amazon SNS natively supports push notifications such as email and SMS. Amazon SQS only queues the failure record for later consumption, and Amazon EventBridge is designed to react to state changes rather than to capture invocation-level execution records directly. The decision logic is: first determine whether the requirement is to store or route failure data for later processing, which points to Amazon SQS or another Lambda function, or whether the requirement is to actively alert people, which points to Amazon SNS.

Applied example: at Amberfield Cooperative, the data engineering team configures an Amazon SNS topic as the on-failure destination for the Lambda function that processes river sensor telemetry from Kinesis. When a batch of sensor records fails to process, Amazon SNS immediately emails the on-call administrators, allowing them to investigate before a gap appears in the compliance reporting data.

Question 47Incorrect

A recent internal audit of client engagement systems revealed that session data across several projects was being stored without a documented capacity plan, creating unpredictable throttling risk during peak assessment periods. In response, Cobalt Labs, a cybersecurity consulting firm, is redesigning its session-storage layer using an Amazon DynamoDB table configured with provisioned capacity mode.

The data being stored is expected to be approximately 4.5 KB in size, and the application will perform 20 eventually consistent reads per second and 12 standard (non-transactional) writes per second.

How many read capacity units (RCUs) and write capacity units (WCUs) are required to support this workload?

40 RCU and 12 WCU

Explanation

Incorrect. The RCU value of 40 in this option matches strongly consistent reads, not the eventually consistent reads stated in the scenario. Strongly consistent reads need twice the RCUs of eventually consistent reads for the same item size and throughput. The WCU value of 12 assumes the entire 4.5 KB item fits inside a single 1 KB write unit, which is incorrect. The item must round up to 5 KB, requiring 5 WCU per write, so 12 writes per second need 60 WCU. Keyword tip: WCU calculations round item size up to the next full 1 KB, so a 4.5 KB item always needs 5 WCU per write, not 1.
Correct answer
20 RCU and 60 WCU

Explanation

Correct. One RCU supports one strongly consistent read per second of an item up to 4 KB. Eventually consistent reads provide double that throughput, so one RCU supports one eventually consistent read per second of an item up to 8 KB after rounding. The 4.5 KB item rounds up to 8 KB, so each read of it consumes one RCU under eventually consistent reads, and 20 reads per second require 20 RCU. For writes, one WCU supports one standard write per second of an item up to 1 KB. The 4.5 KB item rounds up to 5 KB, so each write consumes 5 WCU, and 12 writes per second require 60 WCU. Keyword tip: eventually consistent reads always need half the RCUs of strongly consistent reads for the same rounded item size and read rate.
Your answer is incorrect
40 RCU and 60 WCU

Explanation

Incorrect. This RCU value of 40 is the correct value for strongly consistent reads, not eventually consistent reads. DynamoDB rounds the 4.5 KB item size up to the nearest 4 KB boundary, giving 8 KB. A strongly consistent read of an 8 KB item needs 2 RCU per read, so 20 reads per second need 40 RCU. Eventually consistent reads need only half that number of RCUs for the same item size and throughput. The WCU value of 60 in this option is correct. Keyword tip: the phrase "eventually consistent" always cuts the RCU requirement in half compared to strongly consistent reads of the same item.
10 RCU and 24 WCU

Explanation

Incorrect. This option rounds the item size down instead of up, which DynamoDB never does. The correct process rounds 4.5 KB up to 8 KB for reads and up to 5 KB for writes. Using 10 RCU treats the item as if it were 4 KB after rounding, and using 24 WCU treats the item as if it were 2 KB after rounding, both of which understate the actual capacity needed. Keyword tip: DynamoDB always rounds the item size up to the next boundary, 4 KB for reads and 1 KB for writes, never down.

DynamoDB provisioned capacity requires rounding the item size up to a fixed boundary before applying a per-second throughput formula: reads round up to the nearest 4 KB, and writes round up to the nearest 1 KB. The consistency model then applies a multiplier to the read calculation: strongly consistent reads use 1 RCU per 4 KB unit per read, eventually consistent reads use half that many RCUs for the same throughput, and transactional reads use double the strongly consistent value. Writes follow a similar pattern, where standard writes use 1 WCU per 1 KB unit per write, and transactional writes use double that amount. The correct approach is always to round the item size first, then apply the correct multiplier based on the exact consistency or transaction type named in the scenario.

In practice: a cybersecurity consulting firm like Cobalt Labs often runs many parallel client engagements, each generating session data with predictable read and write patterns. Calculating RCU and WCU precisely before deployment lets the team provision DynamoDB tables that avoid throttling during audits or incident response work, while also avoiding overpaying for unused capacity. Getting the rounding and consistency multiplier wrong is a common real-world cause of both unexpected throttling and unnecessary cost.

Question 48Incorrect

Clearwater Logistics must guarantee that no unencrypted file is ever written to a specific Amazon S3 bucket. The company, a logistics and freight provider that stores sensitive shipment manifests and customs documentation in the clearwater-logistics-freight-docs bucket, has a written policy stating that all data placed in this bucket must be encrypted.

How can a Developer ensure compliance with this policy?

Create an Amazon CloudWatch alarm that notifies an administrator if unencrypted objects are uploaded to the S3 bucket

Explanation

Incorrect. A CloudWatch alarm is a detective control. A detective control reports a problem after the problem already happened. In this case, the alarm would only notify an administrator after an unencrypted object was already stored in the bucket. The policy requires that unencrypted data never be written to the bucket in the first place, so a detective control cannot satisfy this requirement. Keyword tip: alarms and notifications detect problems after the fact; they do not prevent problems from happening.
Your answer is incorrect
Enable Server-Side Encryption with Amazon S3-Managed Keys (SSE-S3) on the Amazon S3 bucket

Explanation

Incorrect. Enabling SSE-S3 sets default encryption on the bucket. Default encryption means Amazon S3 automatically encrypts an object with S3-managed keys only when the upload request does not specify its own encryption method. Default encryption does not reject a request. It only fills in a fallback value when nothing else is specified, so it does not enforce the company's policy. Keyword tip: "default encryption" enables encryption, but it does not enforce or block anything.
Correct answer
Create an S3 bucket policy that denies any S3 Put request that does not include the x-amz-server-side-encryption header

Explanation

Correct. A bucket policy can include a Deny statement that triggers whenever a PutObject request does not include the x-amz-server-side-encryption header. Amazon S3 evaluates this policy before it stores the object. If the header is missing, Amazon S3 rejects the request outright, regardless of whether the intended encryption method was SSE-S3 (AES256) or SSE-KMS (aws:kms). This is the only option that actively blocks a noncompliant upload instead of only enabling encryption or reporting a violation afterward. Keyword tip: a bucket policy Deny condition on the encryption header enforces encryption at upload time, rather than merely enabling it.
Create a bucket policy that denies the S3 PutObject request when the attribute x-amz-acl has values public-read, public-read-write, or authenticated-read

Explanation

Incorrect. This bucket policy statement blocks uploads that set public-facing access control list (ACL) permissions, such as public-read, public-read-write, or authenticated-read. This statement controls who can access an object. It does not check whether the object is encrypted. Keyword tip: x-amz-acl controls object access permissions, not encryption; do not confuse an access-control condition with an encryption condition.

This question tests the difference between enabling encryption and enforcing encryption on Amazon S3. Default bucket encryption (SSE-S3 or SSE-KMS) automatically encrypts an object when the upload request specifies no encryption method, but default encryption never rejects a request, so it cannot guarantee that every object is encrypted the way a strict policy requires. A bucket policy with an explicit Deny statement on the x-amz-server-side-encryption header is evaluated by Amazon S3 before the object is stored, so it can reject any PutObject request that omits the required header. Detective controls, such as a CloudWatch alarm, and access-control conditions, such as an x-amz-acl restriction, address different problems (after-the-fact notification and public access, respectively) and cannot substitute for a preventive encryption policy. When a scenario demands guaranteed compliance rather than a safety net, choose the option that denies the action outright based on a required condition.

A similar situation: Clearwater Logistics stores customs paperwork and shipment manifests for international freight in Amazon S3. Regulators require that this documentation always be encrypted at rest, with no exceptions. By attaching a bucket policy that denies any PutObject request missing the x-amz-server-side-encryption header, Clearwater Logistics guarantees that every file written by its shipping applications, third-party carriers, or automated pipelines is encrypted before Amazon S3 ever stores it, closing the compliance gap that a default-encryption setting alone would leave open.

Question 49Correct

To validate new features safely, a Lambda function must route only 10% of incoming invocation traffic to a new version while the remaining 90% continues to be served by the current version, and no client integration can be changed as part of the rollout. Riverstone Enterprises, a point-of-sale software vendor whose checkout service depends on this Lambda function, needs to implement this gradual traffic split before promoting the new version fully.

Which solution should the team implement to achieve this traffic-shifting requirement?

Your answer is correct
Use AWS Lambda aliases

Explanation

Correct. A Lambda alias is a named pointer to a specific function version. An alias can use weighted alias routing, which lets a team assign a percentage of invocation traffic to two different versions at the same time, for example 90% to the stable version and 10% to the new version, through one alias ARN. This setup enables a gradual, canary-style rollout, and event sources or client applications do not need any reconfiguration when the traffic weights change. Keyword tip: whenever a scenario describes shifting a percentage of traffic between Lambda versions, the answer is aliases with weighted routing.
Use environment variables

Explanation

Incorrect. Environment variables are key-value pairs stored in a function's configuration. Environment variables let a function change its behavior, such as pointing to a different database, without changing the function's code. Environment variables do not control how invocation traffic is split between two function versions. Keyword tip: environment variables are about configuration values, not traffic routing.
Deploy your Lambda function in a VPC

Explanation

Incorrect. Deploying a Lambda function inside a VPC lets the function reach private resources, such as a database in a private network, and adds network isolation. Deploying a function in a VPC has no effect on how traffic is distributed between function versions. Keyword tip: VPC deployment is a networking control, not a traffic-shifting mechanism.
Use tags to distinguish the different versions

Explanation

Incorrect. Tags are freeform key-value labels used to organize Lambda functions for cost allocation, filtering, and billing reports. Tags do not influence which function version is invoked or in what proportion. Keyword tip: tags are for organization and billing, never for routing logic.

This question tests knowledge of Lambda deployment strategies, specifically how to perform canary-style traffic shifting between two function versions. A Lambda alias acts as a stable pointer to a specific version, and an alias supports weighted routing that splits invocation traffic by percentage; this is the standard mechanism for gradual rollouts, and it is often paired with AWS CodeDeploy for automated canary or linear deployment patterns. Environment variables, VPC deployment, and tags each serve a different purpose (configuration, networking, and resource organization), and none of these three options can distribute traffic across function versions. When a scenario describes introducing a new Lambda version to only a fraction of traffic, look for an option that involves aliases, or a CodeDeploy traffic-shifting configuration layered on top of aliases.

A similar situation: Riverstone Enterprises, a point-of-sale software vendor, runs a checkout Lambda function that processes live payment transactions for retail customers. Before the company fully promotes a new version of this function, the development team creates a weighted alias that sends 10% of transaction traffic to the new version and 90% to the current stable version. This approach lets the team monitor error rates and latency on the new version under real transaction load, without changing any client integration or requiring a full cutover.

Question 50Incorrect

The platform engineering team at Kestrel Federation, a smart city government agency that operates traffic and utility monitoring systems, is using an AWS Step Functions state machine to coordinate its sensor-data processing pipeline.

During testing, errors occurred in one of the state machine's task states. To troubleshoot the issue, a developer needs the state output to include both the original state input and the error message that was generated.

Which coding practice should the developer use to preserve both the original input and the error information in the state output?

Use ErrorEquals in a Retry statement to include the original input with the error.

Explanation

Incorrect. ErrorEquals is used inside a Retry or Catch statement. ErrorEquals lists the specific error types that should trigger a retry or a catch action. ErrorEquals does not control how input data and error data are combined in the output. Keyword tip: ErrorEquals identifies which errors match a rule; it does not shape the output JSON.
Correct answer
Use ResultPath in a Catch statement to include the original input with the error.

Explanation

Correct. ResultPath controls where a state places its result inside the output JSON. When a Catch statement captures an error, ResultPath tells Step Functions to add the error information to the existing input instead of replacing the input. This keeps the original input and the error message together in the same output. Keyword tip: when a scenario asks to merge or append an error onto the original input rather than overwrite it, think ResultPath.
Use InputPath in a Catch statement to include the original input with the error.

Explanation

Incorrect. InputPath selects which part of the original input is passed into a state for processing. InputPath does not run inside a Catch statement, and InputPath cannot merge error data with input data. Preserving both the original input and the error requires ResultPath, not InputPath. Keyword tip: InputPath narrows input before processing; ResultPath merges results or errors with input afterward.
Your answer is incorrect
Use OutputPath in a Retry statement to include the original input with the error.

Explanation

Incorrect. OutputPath selects which part of a state's output continues to the next state. OutputPath does not operate inside a Retry statement, and OutputPath cannot combine input data with error data. A Retry statement only controls re-execution attempts after a failure. Keyword tip: OutputPath filters output data; it has no connection to Retry logic.

The Amazon States Language uses several fields to control how JSON data moves between states in a Step Functions workflow: InputPath, OutputPath, ResultPath, Parameters, and ResultSelector. InputPath selects part of the input before a state processes it. OutputPath selects part of the output before the workflow continues to the next state. ResultPath controls how a state's result, including an error captured by a Catch block, gets combined with the original input rather than replacing it. Retry statements, which use ErrorEquals, control re-execution attempts after a failure and play no role in shaping the combined output data.


Consider this scenario: Kestrel Federation runs a Step Functions workflow that ingests readings from thousands of smart city sensors. When a task state fails to parse a malformed sensor reading, the team needs the failed record and the error details stored together for review by the sensor maintenance crew. By adding a Catch statement with ResultPath set to append the error at a specific key, the original sensor payload stays intact in the output alongside the new error information, giving the maintenance crew everything they need in one record.

Question 51Incorrect

Brightwater Dynamics, a cybersecurity consulting firm, uses Amazon CloudFront to deliver on-demand security-awareness training videos stored in an Amazon S3 bucket named brightwater-training-media to enterprise clients worldwide.

The firm is headquartered in Austin, Texas, and its clients access the training platform from many different AWS Regions. Some regions experience noticeable latency whenever a cache miss occurs on CloudFront.

Which configuration change should be recommended to decrease latency and improve user performance by redirecting requests on cache misses to the S3 bucket in the Region nearest to the user's country?

Redirect requests on cache misses to the S3 bucket nearest to the user's country. Create a Lambda@Edge function to redirect requests based on the value of the CloudFront-Viewer-Country header. Associate the Lambda@Edge function with the distribution's viewer request event

Explanation

Incorrect. The viewer request event fires on every single request from the client. This event fires whether the object is cached or not. Attaching the redirection logic to the viewer request event would run the logic on every request, including cache hits. This does not match the requirement to act only on cache misses. Keyword tip: viewer request and viewer response events fire on all requests. Use these events only when the scenario requires the same behavior for every request, not only for cache misses.
Your answer is incorrect
Redirect requests on cache misses to the S3 bucket nearest to the user's country. Create a CloudFront function to redirect requests based on the value of the CloudFront-Viewer-Country header. Associate the CloudFront function with the distribution's origin request event

Explanation

Incorrect. CloudFront Functions support only the viewer request and viewer response events. CloudFront Functions do not support the origin request or origin response events. This option specifies an origin request event, so this option is not technically possible with a CloudFront Function. Keyword tip: CloudFront Functions are lightweight and JavaScript-only, and they are limited strictly to viewer-side events. A question mentioning origin request or origin response events with a CloudFront Function is describing an invalid configuration.
Redirect requests on cache misses to the S3 bucket nearest to the user's country. Create a CloudFront function to redirect requests based on the value of the CloudFront-Viewer-Country header. Associate the CloudFront function with the distribution's viewer request event

Explanation

Incorrect. CloudFront Functions do support the viewer request event, so this configuration is technically valid to create. However, the viewer request event fires on every request, not only on cache misses. This means the redirection logic would run more often than needed. CloudFront Functions also cannot access origin-facing logic, which this use case requires. Keyword tip: when a scenario requires behavior limited strictly to cache misses or requires interaction with the origin, CloudFront Functions are the wrong tool. Lambda@Edge with an origin event is the correct tool.
Correct answer
Redirect requests on cache misses to the S3 bucket nearest to the user's country. Create a Lambda@Edge function to redirect requests based on the value of the CloudFront-Viewer-Country header. Associate the Lambda@Edge function with the distribution's origin request event

Explanation

Correct. The origin request event fires only when CloudFront cannot serve the object from the edge cache. This happens on a cache miss. A Lambda@Edge function attached to the origin request event runs only in that situation. This function can check the CloudFront-Viewer-Country header and redirect the request to the nearest S3 bucket. The redirection logic does not run on cache hits, so there is no wasted invocation. Keyword tip: origin request and origin response events are exclusive to Lambda@Edge and fire only on cache misses. Use this event whenever a question asks for logic that runs only when CloudFront must contact the origin.

CloudFront supports four edge function trigger points: viewer request, viewer response, origin request, and origin response. Viewer events fire on every single request regardless of cache status, while origin events fire only when CloudFront must forward the request to the origin, which happens only on a cache miss. Lambda@Edge supports all four event types, but CloudFront Functions support only the two viewer events. When a requirement states that logic must run only on cache misses or must interact with the origin, the origin request or origin response event is required, and only Lambda@Edge can be attached to those events. The decision always comes down to matching two things: the execution scope needed (all requests versus cache misses only) and which function type supports that specific event.

In practice: a company like Brightwater Dynamics, which serves security-awareness training video content to clients across many countries, wants each client's video request served from the nearest S3 bucket only when that request is not already available from the CloudFront edge cache. Attaching a Lambda@Edge function to the origin request event lets the firm inspect the CloudFront-Viewer-Country header and redirect only cache-miss traffic to the closest regional bucket, keeping cache-hit traffic fast and avoiding unnecessary function invocations.

Question 52Incorrect

Vailmont National, a social media analytics company, ingests real-time engagement metrics from thousands of social media accounts and stores current campaign bid values in Amazon DynamoDB so its bidding engine can adjust ad spend instantly. Multiple worker processes sometimes update the same campaign's bid value at nearly the same moment, and the team has noticed that one worker's update is silently replaced by another worker's update, discarding the first change.

Which approach should the developers implement to stop these updates from overwriting each other?

Use batch operations

Explanation

Incorrect. Batch operations, such as BatchWriteItem, group several write requests into one network call. Batch operations reduce the number of round trips between the application and DynamoDB. Batch operations do not add any conditional check to the individual writes inside the batch. Because batch operations do not check the item's current state, batch operations cannot prevent one worker's update from overwriting another worker's update. Keyword tip: batch operations address network efficiency, not concurrency safety.
Correct answer
Use conditional writes

Explanation

Correct. DynamoDB write operations like PutItem and UpdateItem are unconditional by default. An unconditional write always overwrites the existing item, even if another process changed the item first. A conditional write adds a check before the write happens. The check compares the item's current value to an expected value, such as the bid value the worker originally read. If the current value does not match the expected value, DynamoDB rejects the write and returns an error. This rejection stops one worker's update from silently overwriting another worker's update. Keyword tip: look for phrases like "prevent overwriting concurrent updates" or "ensure updates are not lost" on a DynamoDB item — these phrases point to conditional writes with a condition expression.
Your answer is incorrect
Use atomic counters

Explanation

Incorrect. Atomic counters use the UpdateItem operation to increase or decrease a numeric attribute. Atomic counters do this without checking the attribute's current value first. This makes atomic counters useful for values like a follower count or a like count, where losing an occasional increment is acceptable. Atomic counters do not protect against one bid update overwriting another bid update, because atomic counters never validate the item's prior state. Keyword tip: atomic counters solve unconditional numeric increments, not lost-update protection for arbitrary attribute values.
Use concurrent writes

Explanation

Incorrect. DynamoDB does not have a feature called "concurrent writes." Allowing writes to happen at the same time without any check is the actual cause of the problem in this scenario. Simultaneous unconditional writes can overwrite each other's changes without warning. The correct fix is to add a condition to the write, not to allow more concurrency. Keyword tip: treat any option that describes letting writes happen simultaneously without a check as a distractor in concurrency-control questions.

This question tests optimistic concurrency control in DynamoDB. By default, DynamoDB write operations are unconditional, so the last write always wins, even if that write overwrites a more recent change from another process. Conditional writes solve this problem by adding a condition expression that checks the item's current value before the write happens; if the value does not match what the writer expects, DynamoDB rejects the write instead of overwriting data. Atomic counters and batch operations solve different problems: atomic counters perform unconditional numeric increments, and batch operations group requests together purely for network efficiency, so neither one checks the item's prior state before writing.

Business scenario: Vailmont National's bidding engine runs many worker processes that each read a campaign's current bid value, calculate a new bid, and write the new bid back to DynamoDB. Without a condition expression, two workers that read the same starting bid value can both write their own updated bid, and the second write silently discards the first worker's change. By adding a condition expression that checks the bid value has not changed since the worker last read it, Vailmont National ensures that stale updates are rejected instead of applied, protecting the integrity of its real-time ad spend adjustments.
